steps.title: Distinguish the initial probabilities
steps.body: Before any phenotype information about a child, the genotype probabilities are one quarter AA, one half heterozygous and one quarter aa. Under the stated complete-penetrance model, aa is affected and the other three transmission outcomes are unaffected. These are probabilities for each pregnancy. An affected earlier child does not mechanically use up the affected outcome for a later pregnancy; independent transmissions do not follow a quota.

steps.title: Condition on what is now known
steps.body: If the child is known to be unaffected under this model, the aa outcome is excluded. Three equally likely original transmission outcomes remain: AA, Aa and aA. Two represent carriers. Therefore carrier probability among unaffected children is two thirds, not one half. The denominator changed from all outcomes to the outcomes compatible with the observation. This is an application of conditional probability, not a new rule of meiosis.

steps.title: Respect the model limits
steps.body: The calculation assumes the parental genotypes, the disease model and reliable phenotype classification. Age-dependent or incomplete penetrance can prevent an unaffected observation from excluding aa. Variant interpretation, testing limitations and different genetic mechanisms also matter. A negative test updates probability according to its detection properties; it is not automatically the same evidence as an unaffected phenotype. These exercises teach reasoning and are not individual genetic-risk assessments.

objectives: Construct the Aa × Aa outcome space.
Calculate carrier probability after excluding affected outcomes.
State the assumptions before applying a Mendelian calculation.

workedExample.title: Add a known carrier partner
workedExample.prompt: An unaffected child of two known Aa parents later has a partner known to be Aa. Within the same simplified model, calculate the probability that their child is aa.
solution: The unaffected individual has carrier probability 2/3.
If that individual is Aa, an Aa × Aa cross has aa probability 1/4.
The calculation assumes the same locus, complete penetrance and the stated parental and partner genotypes.

question.prompt: Why is the carrier probability two thirds after an Aa × Aa child is known to be unaffected?

options.text: The recessive allele becomes more likely to segregate
options.reason: Segregation is unchanged; the calculation conditions on an observation.

options.text: Two of four outcomes are carriers
options.reason: That gives the unconditional probability of one half and fails to exclude the affected outcome.

options.text: Two of the three remaining transmission outcomes are heterozygous
options.reason: Excluding aa leaves AA, Aa and aA; two of these three outcomes are carriers.

recall.prompt: Explain the difference between one half and two thirds in this cross.
recall.answer: One half is the carrier probability before learning the child’s phenotype. Two thirds is the carrier probability conditional on being unaffected, assuming aa would always be recognisably affected. Conditioning removes aa from the denominator while retaining both heterozygous transmission outcomes.

lessons.subject: genetics
lessons.title: Hypersensitivity: classify the mechanism of tissue injury
lessons.summary: Distinguish IgE activation, antibody against fixed targets, immune complexes and T-cell responses through original comparison cases.
tags: Hypersensitivity: classify the mechanism of tissue injury
lessons.section: Immunology teaching sections: antibodies, effector mechanisms and hypersensitivity

steps.title: Start with the cause of injury
steps.body: Hypersensitivity describes immune responses that cause tissue damage. The traditional four-type framework organises mechanisms; a real disorder can involve more than one. Classification requires identifying antigen location, effector molecules or cells, and the process causing injury. The words rapid and delayed are clues, but timing by itself is not a complete mechanism. Do not call every inflammatory response IgE-mediated allergy.

steps.title: Connect IgE with a sensitised mast cell
steps.body: In type I reactions, antigen cross-links specific IgE already bound to high-affinity receptors on mast cells or basophils. This triggers mediator release and subsequent inflammatory events. Sensitisation and the later effector response are distinct stages. An immediate component can be followed by later inflammation, so a later phase does not automatically convert the response into type IV. The key is the IgE-linked activation pathway.

steps.title: Distinguish the two antibody patterns
steps.body: Type II involves antibodies directed against cell-surface or extracellular-matrix targets. Effects can include complement activation, phagocyte-mediated injury or altered receptor function; cell destruction is not the only possible result. Type III involves antigen–antibody complexes whose deposition and associated inflammation injure tissues. Ask whether the antibody targets a fixed structure directly or whether complexes form and deposit. Both may recruit complement, so complement alone cannot separate them.

steps.title: Recognise a T-cell effector response
steps.body: Type IV responses are mediated principally by antigen-specific T cells. CD4 T-cell cytokines can recruit and activate inflammatory cells, while CD8 T cells can injure target cells directly. Contact dermatitis is a classic teaching context. The time needed for recruitment helps explain a delayed response, but the defining feature is the effector mechanism. Naming a cytokine or a time interval without identifying the cells leaves the explanation incomplete.

objectives: Identify the effector rather than classify by timing alone.
Separate fixed-target antibodies from deposited immune complexes.
Explain why type IV does not require antibody as its principal effector.

workedExample.title: Classify an original comparison case
workedExample.prompt: Case A: antibody binds a receptor and changes its function. Case B: soluble antigen–antibody complexes deposit and recruit inflammatory cells. Case C: sensitised T cells drive local inflammation after contact exposure.
solution: A follows a type II mechanism because antibody acts against a fixed target; receptor effects need not lyse the cell.
B follows a type III mechanism because deposited complexes drive the injury.
C follows a type IV mechanism because T cells are the principal specific effectors.

question.prompt: Which distinction best separates type II from type III injury?

options.text: Antibody against a fixed target versus deposited immune complexes
options.reason: The location and form of the antigen–antibody interaction distinguish these mechanisms.

options.text: Any complement activation versus no complement activation
options.reason: Complement can contribute to both, so this distinction is unreliable.
Microbial category does not define the type II/type III division.

recall.prompt: Give a mechanism-first comparison of all four types.
recall.answer: Type I links antigen to IgE-bearing effector cells. Type II links antibody to a fixed cellular or matrix target and can change receptor function or cause injury. Type III links deposited immune complexes to inflammation. Type IV uses antigen-specific T cells as the main effectors. Actual disorders may combine pathways.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Radiation, units and geometric optics
lessons.summary: Distinguish waves from particles, quantify a beam and predict reflection or refraction.
lessons.section: Medical Biophysics I, topic 1; combined theory prompts 1–9

steps.title: Describe what travels
steps.body: Radiation transports energy away from a source. Electromagnetic radiation can propagate through vacuum; sound requires matter. Photons carry energy hf and momentum h/λ, whereas massive particles also have rest mass. Neither visible light nor an ultrasound wave should be described as a stream of electrons.

steps.title: Measure the beam
steps.body: Radiant energy is measured in joules and radiant power in watts. Irradiance is power per receiving area, in W/m²; radiant intensity is power per solid angle, in W/sr. For an isotropic point source without attenuation, irradiance falls as 1/r². Tilting a surface introduces a cosine factor in intercepted power.

steps.title: Trace a ray
steps.body: Geometric optics applies when wavelength is small relative to the relevant structures. Fermat's stationary optical-path principle leads to reflection and Snell's law: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂, with angles measured from the normal. At a boundary frequency stays fixed; wavelength and speed change together.

steps.title: Work the boundary
steps.body: A ray travelling from glass with n = 1.50 into air has critical angle arcsin(1/1.50) ≈ 41.8°. Total internal reflection requires incidence above that angle and travel toward the lower-index medium. This explains fibre guidance; it cannot occur for light entering glass from air.

steps.title: Check the model
steps.body: A doubled distance gives one quarter the irradiance only for the point-source model. Refraction does not mean every ray reaches the second medium: reflection may occur simultaneously. At apertures comparable with wavelength, use wave optics rather than extending ray diagrams beyond their assumptions.

question.prompt: A point source is moved from 1 m to 3 m. Ignoring attenuation, what fraction of irradiance remains?

options.reason: Irradiance scales as 1/r², so the ratio is 1/3².
Irradiance depends on squared distance, not distance alone.
Moving farther away reduces irradiance in this model.

recall.prompt: Explain radiation, units and geometric optics: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: Irradiance scales as 1/r², so the ratio is 1/3². Both index ordering and an angle above the critical angle are required. A doubled distance gives one quarter the irradiance only for the point-source model. Refraction does not mean every ray reaches the second medium: reflection may occur simultaneously. At apertures comparable with wavelength, use wave optics rather than extending ray diagrams beyond their assumptions.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Lenses, magnification and the microscope
lessons.summary: Construct real and virtual images and separate magnification from useful optical detail.
lessons.section: Medical Biophysics I, topic 2; combined theory prompts 10–18

steps.title: Choose a sign convention
steps.body: For a thin lens in air, use 1/f = 1/u + 1/v with u positive for a real object and v positive for a real image on the outgoing side. A converging lens has positive f. State the convention before interpreting a negative value; diagrams and equations must describe the same geometry.

steps.title: Construct the image
steps.body: Trace a parallel ray through the far focus and a central ray approximately undeviated. An object beyond f gives a real inverted image; one inside f gives a virtual upright enlarged image. Exactly at f the emerging rays are parallel. A virtual image is located by backward extensions and cannot be caught directly on a screen.

steps.title: Combine optical elements
steps.body: Power P = 1/f in metres is measured in dioptres. Powers add for thin lenses in contact, but separation changes the equivalent system. A microscope objective forms an enlarged intermediate image; an eyepiece acts as a magnifier. Total nominal magnification is the product, whereas resolution depends on wavelength and numerical aperture.

steps.title: Calculate an image
steps.body: For f = 10 cm and u = 30 cm, 1/v = 1/10 − 1/30, so v = 15 cm. Magnification m = −v/u = −0.5: the real image is inverted and half the object height. The lens power is +10 D, because f = 0.10 m.

steps.title: Connect to the eye
steps.body: The cornea and lens focus a real inverted image on the retina. Accommodation changes lens power; it does not move a screen-like retina. Spherical and chromatic aberrations are departures from the ideal thin-lens model. Enlarging an already blurred image adds size without recovering lost spatial information.

question.prompt: A converging lens has f = 0.25 m. What is its power?

options.reason: A converging lens in this convention has positive power.
1/0.25 m = +4 m⁻¹, or +4 dioptres.
Power is the reciprocal of focal length in metres.

recall.prompt: Explain lenses, magnification and the microscope: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: 1/0.25 m = +4 m⁻¹, or +4 dioptres. Inside the focal length, backward ray extensions locate an enlarged upright virtual image. The cornea and lens focus a real inverted image on the retina. Accommodation changes lens power; it does not move a screen-like retina. Spherical and chromatic aberrations are departures from the ideal thin-lens model. Enlarging an already blurred image adds size without recovering lost spatial information.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Interference, diffraction and optical resolution
lessons.summary: Use phase, wavelength and aperture to explain what an optical instrument can distinguish.
lessons.section: Medical Biophysics I, topic 3; combined theory prompts 19–28

steps.title: Track phase
steps.body: A harmonic oscillation repeats with frequency f and period 1/f. A travelling wave obeys v = fλ. Superposition adds amplitudes, including their signs and phases: equal coherent waves can reinforce or cancel. Stable interference requires a sufficiently stable phase relationship, not merely two beams of the same colour.

steps.title: Explain diffraction
steps.body: Huygens–Fresnel reasoning treats each part of a wavefront as contributing secondary waves. A finite aperture spreads light; narrowing it generally broadens the diffraction pattern. For a grating at normal incidence, d sin θ = mλ locates principal maxima. Different wavelengths therefore emerge at different angles.

steps.title: Distinguish resolution from magnification
steps.body: A common microscope estimate is d ≈ 0.61λ/NA, where NA = n sin α and α is the collection half-angle. Shorter wavelength or larger numerical aperture reduces the resolvable spacing. This is a model-dependent criterion, not a promise that every specimen will show that detail despite noise and poor contrast.

steps.title: Use polarisation and phase
steps.body: Linear polarisation specifies the electric-field orientation. An ideal analyser transmits intensity I = I₀ cos²θ for linearly polarised input. Birefringent material gives different phase delays to orthogonal components. A phase-contrast microscope converts specimen phase differences into visible intensity differences, enabling observation of weakly absorbing structures.

steps.title: Work a comparison
steps.body: At fixed NA, changing illumination from 600 nm to 450 nm reduces the estimated resolution distance to 450/600 = 0.75 of its former value. A stronger eyepiece alone does not change this distance. Draw both the specimen spacing and diffraction spots before claiming that two points are resolved.

question.prompt: At fixed wavelength, what happens when numerical aperture doubles?

options.reason: Numerical aperture is in the denominator of the resolution estimate.
Aperture changes diffraction-limited resolution, not just displayed size.
In d ≈ 0.61λ/NA, doubling NA halves d.

recall.prompt: Explain interference, diffraction and optical resolution: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: In d ≈ 0.61λ/NA, doubling NA halves d. Malus's law gives cos²90° = 0 for crossed linear axes. At fixed NA, changing illumination from 600 nm to 450 nm reduces the estimated resolution distance to 450/600 = 0.75 of its former value. A stronger eyepiece alone does not change this distance. Draw both the specimen spacing and diffraction spots before claiming that two points are resolved.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Photons, matter waves and electron microscopy
lessons.summary: Connect interference and quantised energy transfer without confusing their experimental evidence.
lessons.section: Medical Biophysics I, topic 4; combined theory prompts 29–37

steps.title: Separate the experiments
steps.body: Interference reveals wave behaviour; the photoelectric effect reveals quantised energy exchange. Increasing light intensity increases photon arrival rate at a fixed frequency. Increasing frequency increases each photon's energy. One description is not a licence to use a classical wave-energy argument for the photoelectric threshold.

steps.title: Apply the photoelectric equation
steps.body: The maximum emitted electron kinetic energy is Kmax = hf − φ, where φ is the material's work function. Below threshold hf < φ, increasing intensity does not produce ordinary single-photon photoemission. Above threshold, intensity mainly changes the number of emitted electrons, not their maximum kinetic energy.

steps.title: Compare matter waves
steps.body: A particle with momentum p has de Broglie wavelength λ = h/p. Electron diffraction demonstrates that this relation is experimentally meaningful. Electron microscopes use accelerated electrons and electromagnetic lenses; their short wavelengths permit high resolution, but specimen preparation, lens aberrations and beam damage constrain useful detail.

steps.title: Work a photon example
steps.body: Using hc ≈ 1240 eV·nm, a 400 nm photon carries 3.10 eV. If the work function is 2.00 eV, the maximum photoelectron energy is 1.10 eV. Doubling photon flux doubles the potential event rate in an ideal unsaturated detector without changing this maximum energy.

steps.title: Connect momentum to force
steps.body: Light changes momentum when absorbed or redirected. Optical traps use focused-beam forces to confine suitable small particles; heating, particle refractive properties and geometry matter. The electromagnetic spectrum orders frequency and wavelength continuously: labels such as visible or X-ray do not introduce a new photon energy law.

question.prompt: Above threshold, light frequency is fixed and intensity doubles. What changes most directly?

options.reason: More photons can eject more electrons while the maximum energy stays fixed.
Maximum energy is set by hf minus work function.
The work function is a property of the surface, not light intensity.

recall.prompt: Explain photons, matter waves and electron microscopy: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: More photons can eject more electrons while the maximum energy stays fixed. The relation λ = h/p predicts half the wavelength. Light changes momentum when absorbed or redirected. Optical traps use focused-beam forces to confine suitable small particles; heating, particle refractive properties and geometry matter. The electromagnetic spectrum orders frequency and wavelength continuously: labels such as visible or X-ray do not introduce a new photon energy law.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Atomic models, energy levels and uncertainty
lessons.summary: Use historical models to identify what each experiment explains and what it cannot.
lessons.section: Medical Biophysics I, topic 5; combined theory prompts 38–44

steps.title: Follow the evidence
steps.body: Dalton's atom model organised chemical composition; Thomson introduced embedded electrons; scattering experiments required a small concentrated positive nucleus. A classical planetary electron would radiate and collapse, so it cannot explain stable atomic structure. Model revision follows a failed prediction, not simply a more detailed drawing.

steps.title: Quantise energy
steps.body: Bohr's hydrogen model allows selected energies and photons with hf = |ΔE| between levels. It explains important hydrogen spectral features but does not supply a general picture of multi-electron atoms. The quantum model uses orbitals as probability distributions, not narrow tracks traversed by miniature planets.

steps.title: Use quantum numbers
steps.body: Principal, angular-momentum, magnetic and spin quantum numbers organise electron states. Pauli exclusion prevents two electrons in an atom from sharing the full set. Shell filling, effective nuclear charge and shielding help explain periodic chemical properties. An orbital's spatial extent is different from a measured instantaneous electron position.

steps.title: Interpret uncertainty
steps.body: The relation Δx Δp ≥ ħ/2 constrains a state's position and momentum spreads. It is not merely a poor microscope or a statement that electrons have no measurable properties. Wave packets require a range of momenta to localise a particle; tighter localisation broadens that distribution.

steps.title: Read experimental transitions
steps.body: In a Franck–Hertz-type experiment, electrons lose discrete amounts of energy when exciting atoms. A 5 eV excitation would correspond to a photon of roughly 248 nm if the atom returned directly by emitting one photon. Multiple allowed decay pathways can produce several spectral lines instead.

question.prompt: What does an atomic orbital represent?

options.reason: Electronic orbitals describe electron states.

options.text: A quantum state with a spatial probability distribution
options.reason: An orbital supports predictions about measurement probabilities rather than a fixed electron path.
Orbitals are not classical planetary trajectories.

recall.prompt: Explain atomic models, energy levels and uncertainty: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: An orbital supports predictions about measurement probabilities rather than a fixed electron path. E = hc/λ makes doubled energy correspond to halved wavelength. In a Franck–Hertz-type experiment, electrons lose discrete amounts of energy when exciting atoms. A 5 eV excitation would correspond to a photon of roughly 248 nm if the atom returned directly by emitting one photon. Multiple allowed decay pathways can produce several spectral lines instead.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Bonds, interaction energies and scanning probes
lessons.summary: Connect the shape of an interaction potential to molecular structure and measurement.
lessons.section: Medical Biophysics I, topic 6; combined theory prompts 45–49

steps.title: Read an energy curve
steps.body: A stable separation lies near a potential-energy minimum where net force is zero and curvature is positive. Attraction dominates over one distance range and steep repulsion prevents unlimited approach. Force is the negative spatial derivative of potential energy: zero potential is not the same thing as zero force.

steps.title: Compare chemical interactions
steps.body: Covalent bonding involves shared electron density; ionic interactions involve charges and depend strongly on the medium. Electronegativity differences help predict bond polarity. Hydrogen bonds are directional interactions involving suitable donors and acceptors. Dispersion forces occur even in nonpolar molecules through fluctuating charge distributions.

steps.title: Connect many weak interactions
steps.body: Thermal energy kBT competes with interaction energies. Individually modest noncovalent contacts can stabilise a large macromolecule when many act together. Solvent and entropy affect the free-energy balance, so counting bonds alone does not predict whether a complex forms. Hydrophobic association is a solvent-related effect rather than a new covalent bond.

steps.title: Measure surfaces
steps.body: Scanning tunnelling microscopy senses a tunnelling current that depends sharply on tip–sample separation and electronic states, requiring a suitable conducting pathway. Atomic force microscopy senses tip forces through a cantilever and can study insulating samples. Neither instrument produces an ordinary colour photograph of atoms.

steps.title: Predict a perturbation
steps.body: Moving particles slightly away from a stable minimum produces a restoring tendency. Raising temperature may increase fluctuations enough to disrupt weak associations, but no single temperature applies to every interaction. For a probe image, ask whether apparent height reflects topography, electronic structure or the chosen force-feedback mode.

question.prompt: Where is a stable equilibrium on a potential-energy graph?

options.text: At every point where potential equals zero
options.reason: The zero of potential can be chosen arbitrarily.
A small displacement from a maximum tends to grow.
A local minimum has restoring forces for small displacements.

recall.prompt: Explain bonds, interaction energies and scanning probes: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: A local minimum has restoring forces for small displacements. AFM measures interaction forces and does not require a tunnelling current. Moving particles slightly away from a stable minimum produces a restoring tendency. Raising temperature may increase fluctuations enough to disrupt weak associations, but no single temperature applies to every interaction. For a probe image, ask whether apparent height reflects topography, electronic structure or the chosen force-feedback mode.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Gas laws, Boltzmann statistics and thermal energy
lessons.summary: Move between molecular motion, bulk pressure and equilibrium populations.
lessons.section: Medical Biophysics I, topic 7; combined theory prompts 50–62

steps.title: Connect microscopic motion to pressure
steps.body: Gas pressure comes from momentum transfer in collisions with container walls. For a dilute ideal gas, pV = NkBT = nRT. Absolute temperature is required. The model neglects molecular volume and intermolecular potential energy; high density and proximity to condensation make those assumptions unreliable.

steps.title: Describe speeds statistically
steps.body: A Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution describes speeds in a classical equilibrium gas. Molecules do not all share the mean speed. Raising temperature broadens the distribution and shifts characteristic speeds upward; heavier particles have lower characteristic speeds at the same temperature. Mean translational energy is 3kBT/2 per particle.

steps.title: Compare energy populations
steps.body: For equal degeneracy, relative occupation of two states is exp(−ΔE/kBT). Larger energy gaps reduce high-energy occupation, while warming makes it less strongly suppressed. Barometric density variation is a spatial version of this balance in gravity. Degeneracy must be included when states have unequal multiplicity.

steps.title: Recognise nonideal behaviour
steps.body: The van der Waals equation introduces finite molecular volume and attractive forces. These corrections explain why an ideal-gas extrapolation can fail. At equilibrium chemical reactions balance forward and reverse rates; Arrhenius temperature dependence describes barrier crossing, not proof that every collision reacts.

steps.title: Work and interpret
steps.body: An ideal gas warmed from 300 K to 330 K at fixed volume has pressure multiplied by 330/300 = 1.10. Celsius temperatures would give the wrong ratio. Entropy S = kB ln Ω connects accessible microstates with bulk thermodynamics, but Ω must refer to states consistent with the specified macroscopic constraints.

question.prompt: At fixed volume, an ideal gas warms from 300 K to 600 K. Its pressure…

options.reason: p = NkBT/V gives a twofold increase.
Fixed volume does not fix pressure when temperature changes.
Pressure is proportional, not inversely proportional, to absolute temperature.

recall.prompt: Explain gas laws, boltzmann statistics and thermal energy: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: p = NkBT/V gives a twofold increase. exp(−ΔE/kBT) decreases as a positive ΔE increases. An ideal gas warmed from 300 K to 330 K at fixed volume has pressure multiplied by 330/300 = 1.10. Celsius temperatures would give the wrong ratio. Entropy S = kB ln Ω connects accessible microstates with bulk thermodynamics, but Ω must refer to states consistent with the specified macroscopic constraints.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Solids, liquids, liquid crystals and energy bands
lessons.summary: Explain material properties from molecular order and accessible electronic states.
lessons.section: Medical Biophysics I, topic 8; combined theory prompts 63–73

steps.title: Compare forms of order
steps.body: A crystal has long-range positional order; an amorphous solid lacks that periodic arrangement. Liquids retain short-range correlations while molecules rearrange. Liquid crystals combine fluidity with partial orientational or positional order, so their response depends on direction. A biological membrane is not a rigid three-dimensional crystal.

steps.title: Distinguish liquid-crystal classes
steps.body: Thermotropic phases change principally with temperature. Lyotropic phases depend on composition and solvent concentration as well as temperature. Anisotropy can alter optical propagation; applied fields can reorient suitable molecules, changing transmitted light between polarisers. This is an electro-optical effect, not light being electrically charged.

steps.title: Use the band picture
steps.body: Closely spaced atomic states form bands in a solid. Conductors have accessible nearby states for mobile carriers; insulators have a substantial gap between occupied and accessible empty bands. Semiconductors have a smaller relevant gap. Conductivity depends on both carrier concentration and mobility, not just the number of atoms.

steps.title: Compare intrinsic and doped material
steps.body: Thermal excitation in an intrinsic semiconductor creates electrons and holes. Donor and acceptor dopants favour electron or hole conduction. Both carrier types contribute according to their concentration and mobility. Temperature may increase carrier density while also changing scattering, so different materials need not share one simple conductivity trend.

steps.title: Apply the distinction
steps.body: A thermistor uses a reproducible resistance–temperature relationship; it requires calibration rather than an assumption that every resistance doubles with temperature. A liquid-crystal display controls optical transmission by changing molecular alignment. Describe the measured quantity and the intervening mechanism before treating either device as a direct thermometer or light source.

question.prompt: Why can a liquid crystal have direction-dependent optical properties?

options.text: Light acquires electric charge inside it
options.reason: Optical anisotropy does not require charging photons.

options.text: Its molecules retain partial orientational order
options.reason: Partial order makes the optical response depend on orientation.

options.text: Every molecule occupies a rigid crystal lattice
options.reason: Liquid-crystal phases retain fluidity and need not have full positional order.

recall.prompt: Explain solids, liquids, liquid crystals and energy bands: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: Partial order makes the optical response depend on orientation. Acceptor doping increases hole availability in a p-type semiconductor. A thermistor uses a reproducible resistance–temperature relationship; it requires calibration rather than an assumption that every resistance doubles with temperature. A liquid-crystal display controls optical transmission by changing molecular alignment. Describe the measured quantity and the intervening mechanism before treating either device as a direct thermometer or light source.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Absorption, scattering and optical spectroscopy
lessons.summary: Separate loss mechanisms and use a spectrum to infer molecular information.
lessons.section: Medical Biophysics I, topic 9; combined theory prompts 74–80

steps.title: Track the missing beam
steps.body: A detector placed directly behind a sample measures transmitted light. Reduced transmission can reflect absorption, scattering out of the beam or reflection. Only absorbed energy is necessarily transferred internally to the sample. Geometry and collection optics determine whether scattered light contributes to the measured signal.

steps.title: Apply Beer–Lambert carefully
steps.body: For a homogeneous non-scattering dilute solution under suitable monochromatic conditions, A = log₁₀(I₀/I) = εcl. Absorbance is dimensionless, c is concentration and l is path length; ε must use compatible units. A blank corrects for solvent and container contributions, not for every possible sample artifact.

steps.title: Explain spectral structure
steps.body: Molecules absorb when photon energy matches allowed electronic, vibrational or rotational transitions. A spectrometer separates wavelengths and measures a response across them. Broad molecular bands differ from isolated atomic lines. Peaks alone may not identify a compound uniquely, especially when several absorbing species overlap.

steps.title: Compare scattering
steps.body: Rayleigh scattering applies to particles much smaller than wavelength and has a strong inverse wavelength dependence. Mie scattering describes larger spherical-particle regimes with more complex angular behaviour. Dynamic light scattering analyses fluctuations caused by particle motion, linking correlation times to diffusion under a model rather than directly photographing particle diameters.

steps.title: Work a transmission result
steps.body: If I/I₀ = 0.01, absorbance is 2. Increasing concentration twofold at fixed ε and l predicts A = 4, or transmission 0.0001. Such tiny signals may exceed useful instrument range because stray light and noise matter. A linear equation does not guarantee reliable measurements at arbitrary concentration.

question.prompt: A sample transmits 10% of the blank intensity. Its absorbance is…

options.reason: Transmission fraction and logarithmic absorbance are different quantities.
Absorbance is log₁₀(1/0.1), not its unlogged ratio.
A = −log₁₀0.1 = 1.

recall.prompt: Explain absorption, scattering and optical spectroscopy: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: A = −log₁₀0.1 = 1. A transmission measurement alone does not separate absorption from scattering losses. If I/I₀ = 0.01, absorbance is 2. Increasing concentration twofold at fixed ε and l predicts A = 4, or transmission 0.0001. Such tiny signals may exceed useful instrument range because stray light and noise matter. A linear equation does not guarantee reliable measurements at arbitrary concentration.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Blackbody radiation and thermal imaging
lessons.summary: Relate a temperature distribution to emitted power and spectral shape.
lessons.section: Medical Biophysics I, topic 10; combined theory prompts 81–89

steps.title: Define an ideal reference
steps.body: A blackbody absorbs incident radiation completely and emits a temperature-dependent equilibrium spectrum. Real surfaces are described using emissivity, which can depend on wavelength, angle and temperature. A dark appearance in visible light does not automatically imply identical behaviour in thermal infrared.

steps.title: Read the laws together
steps.body: Planck's law gives the spectral distribution. Wien's wavelength displacement law gives λmax T ≈ 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K. Stefan–Boltzmann gives total blackbody radiant exitance M = σT⁴. The peak location and total area describe different aspects of one spectrum; use kelvin in both relations.

steps.title: Account for surroundings
steps.body: For an idealised grey surface exchanging radiation with a large enclosure, net power is approximately εσA(T⁴ − Tenv⁴). Emission alone is not net cooling because the body also absorbs radiation. Kirchhoff's relation links emissivity and absorptivity at thermal equilibrium under corresponding spectral and directional conditions.

steps.title: Work a thermal scale
steps.body: At 300 K, Wien's relation gives a peak near 9.7 μm, in the infrared. Doubling absolute temperature multiplies ideal total emitted power per area by 16 and halves peak wavelength. A small rise around body temperature is not equivalent to doubling kelvin temperature.

steps.title: Interpret an image
steps.body: A thermal camera estimates apparent surface temperature from detected infrared radiation and assumptions about emissivity and surroundings. Reflections, sweat, coverings and environment affect readings. The image represents surface radiance, not a direct map of deep internal temperature or a diagnosis by colour alone.

question.prompt: An ideal blackbody's absolute temperature doubles. Total emitted power per area changes by…

options.reason: Stefan–Boltzmann scaling gives 2⁴ = 16.
Total emission follows the fourth power, not a linear law.
The peak wavelength halves, but total emission rises.

recall.prompt: Explain blackbody radiation and thermal imaging: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: Stefan–Boltzmann scaling gives 2⁴ = 16. Net exchange subtracts incoming absorbed radiation from outgoing emission. A thermal camera estimates apparent surface temperature from detected infrared radiation and assumptions about emissivity and surroundings. Reflections, sweat, coverings and environment affect readings. The image represents surface radiance, not a direct map of deep internal temperature or a diagnosis by colour alone.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Fluorescence, phosphorescence and molecular probes
lessons.summary: Follow excitation and relaxation pathways to interpret luminescence measurements.
lessons.section: Medical Biophysics I, topic 11; combined theory prompts 90–102

steps.title: Build an energy diagram
steps.body: Absorption promotes a molecule into an excited state. Vibrational relaxation and internal conversion can reduce its energy without photon emission. Fluorescence commonly occurs from the lowest excited singlet state to the ground state, consistent with Kasha's rule in many molecules. Exceptions exist, so the rule is not an absolute prohibition.

steps.title: Distinguish delayed emission
steps.body: Intersystem crossing changes spin multiplicity and can populate a triplet state. Phosphorescence commonly involves a spin-forbidden triplet-to-singlet transition and is often longer lived than fluorescence. Both are luminescence; neither requires a body to have the blackbody temperature corresponding to the emitted colour.

steps.title: Measure yield and lifetime
steps.body: Quantum yield is emitted photons divided by absorbed photons. Lifetime describes excited-state population decay, often approximately exponential. Nonradiative pathways reduce yield and can shorten lifetime. Intensity also depends on illumination, concentration, collection and detector response, so dim emission alone does not uniquely identify the cause.

steps.title: Separate excitation from detection
steps.body: A fluorimeter selects excitation and observes emission with spectral separation, often using a right-angle geometry to reduce direct excitation light. Fluorescence microscopy uses labels and filters to localise signals. A Stokes shift places common emission at longer wavelength than excitation because some energy is lost before photon emission.

steps.title: Work a decay
steps.body: For a single lifetime τ = 4 ns, the excited population remaining after 4 ns is e⁻¹ ≈ 37%. A 40% quantum yield means about 40 emitted photons per 100 absorbed on average, not that every molecule emits a photon with 40% of the excitation energy.

question.prompt: A quantum yield of 0.25 means…

options.reason: Quantum yield is dimensionless and does not specify lifetime.

options.text: About 25 photons emitted per 100 absorbed on average
options.reason: Quantum yield compares emitted and absorbed photon numbers.

options.text: Each photon has one quarter the excitation energy
options.reason: Yield counts photons; it is not a photon-energy fraction.

recall.prompt: Explain fluorescence, phosphorescence and molecular probes: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: Quantum yield compares emitted and absorbed photon numbers. Relaxation before emission reduces photon energy and increases wavelength. For a single lifetime τ = 4 ns, the excited population remaining after 4 ns is e⁻¹ ≈ 37%. A 40% quantum yield means about 40 emitted photons per 100 absorbed on average, not that every molecule emits a photon with 40% of the excitation energy.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Stimulated emission and medical laser principles
lessons.summary: Explain how pumping and feedback produce a laser beam and why tissue response varies.
lessons.section: Medical Biophysics I, topic 12; combined theory prompts 103–108

steps.title: Compare emission processes
steps.body: Spontaneous emission occurs without an incoming matching photon. Stimulated emission is induced by the electromagnetic field and adds radiation in the stimulating mode. Absorption competes with gain. Population inversion supplies more emitters than absorbers for the relevant laser transition; thermal equilibrium alone does not normally provide it.

steps.title: Build the device
steps.body: A pump transfers energy into the active medium. Metastable states can help sustain inversion, while an optical resonator provides feedback and selects modes. An output coupler lets part of the light leave. Gas, solid-state and semiconductor lasers use different media and pumping arrangements but share the need for gain and controlled losses.

steps.title: Interpret beam properties
steps.body: Laser light can be highly directional, spectrally narrow and coherent, but those properties have finite limits. Continuous and pulsed operation differ in peak power and timing. Average power equals pulse energy times repetition rate for a regular pulse train; a low average power can still accompany a high short-pulse peak.

steps.title: Connect wavelength to tissue
steps.body: Absorption by water, pigments and other chromophores determines where energy is deposited. Heating, photochemical effects and mechanical disruption depend on wavelength, irradiance and exposure time. The word laser alone does not specify depth, effect or clinical suitability. Eye exposure risk also depends on focusing and wavelength.

steps.title: Work a pulse train
steps.body: A teaching source emits 2 mJ pulses at 100 pulses/s. Average power is 0.002 J × 100/s = 0.2 W. If each pulse lasts 1 μs with an ideal flat profile, pulse power is 2000 W. These are different descriptors; neither calculation defines a treatment setting.

question.prompt: What supplies the energy for sustained laser emission?

options.reason: Mirrors provide feedback but do not supply energy.
Coherence does not remove the need for an energy source.

options.text: The pump acting on the gain medium
options.reason: Pumping maintains gain against losses and extracted output.

recall.prompt: Explain stimulated emission and medical laser principles: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: Pumping maintains gain against losses and extracted output. 0.001 J × 500/s = 0.5 W. A teaching source emits 2 mJ pulses at 100 pulses/s. Average power is 0.002 J × 100/s = 0.2 W. If each pulse lasts 1 μs with an ideal flat profile, pulse power is 2000 W. These are different descriptors; neither calculation defines a treatment setting.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Nuclei, isotopes and radioactive transformations
lessons.summary: Identify nuclear changes from conservation laws rather than memorising radiation names.
lessons.section: Medical Biophysics I, topic 13; combined theory prompts 109–119

steps.title: Identify the nucleus
steps.body: Atomic number Z counts protons; mass number A counts protons plus neutrons. Isotopes share Z but differ in neutron number. Nuclear stability reflects competing interactions and neutron–proton balance; binding energy per nucleon helps compare nuclear configurations. Atomic chemistry and nuclear transformation are distinct processes.

steps.title: Balance charged-particle decay
steps.body: Alpha emission lowers A by 4 and Z by 2. In beta-minus decay a neutron becomes a proton with an electron and antineutrino emitted, leaving A unchanged and increasing Z by 1. Beta-plus decay lowers Z by 1 with a positron and neutrino emitted; electron capture also lowers Z by 1.

steps.title: Separate de-excitation
steps.body: Gamma emission releases nuclear excitation energy without changing A or Z. A daughter may remain excited after another decay and subsequently emit gamma radiation. Beta spectra are continuous because energy is shared with another emitted particle; many alpha and gamma emissions have characteristic discrete energies.

steps.title: Explain production
steps.body: Radionuclides can be produced by nuclear reactions in reactors or accelerators, or obtained from decay of a parent in a generator. The daughter element follows charge and nucleon bookkeeping. Production route, chemical separation, purity and half-life all influence whether a radionuclide is useful as a tracer.

steps.title: Work nuclear bookkeeping
steps.body: An alpha decay of a nucleus with A = 226 and Z = 88 produces a daughter with A = 222 and Z = 86. A following gamma emission leaves those numbers unchanged. Do not subtract four electrons or interpret a gamma photon as a lost nucleon.

question.prompt: Beta-minus decay changes the daughter atomic number by…

options.reason: A neutron converts into a proton, increasing Z without changing A.
That direction applies to beta-plus decay or electron capture.
That bookkeeping describes alpha decay.

recall.prompt: Explain nuclei, isotopes and radioactive transformations: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: A neutron converts into a proton, increasing Z without changing A. The nucleus moves to a lower energy state without changing its composition. An alpha decay of a nucleus with A = 226 and Z = 88 produces a daughter with A = 222 and Z = 86. A following gamma emission leaves those numbers unchanged. Do not subtract four electrons or interpret a gamma photon as a lost nucleon.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Decay law and radiation interactions with matter
lessons.summary: Calculate activity changes and distinguish how different radiations deposit energy.
lessons.section: Medical Biophysics I, topic 14; combined theory prompts 120–128

steps.title: Use the decay law
steps.body: For one radionuclide, N(t) = N₀exp(−λt) and activity A(t) = λN(t). Activity is measured in becquerels, meaning decays per second. Half-life T½ = ln 2/λ and mean lifetime τ = 1/λ are different. Individual decays are random even though large populations follow a predictable statistical curve.

steps.title: Track charged particles
steps.body: Alpha particles produce dense ionisation over a short range. Electrons and positrons lose energy through interactions with matter; positrons eventually annihilate with electrons, commonly producing two approximately 511 keV photons. Fast protons have a depth-dependent energy deposition with a Bragg peak near the end of their range.

steps.title: Distinguish photon mechanisms
steps.body: Photoelectric absorption transfers photon energy to an electron, with binding-energy bookkeeping. Compton scattering transfers some energy to an electron and leaves a redirected lower-energy photon. Pair production requires at least 1.022 MeV near a suitable interaction partner, producing an electron and positron.

steps.title: Apply attenuation
steps.body: A narrow monoenergetic photon beam can follow I = I₀exp(−μx) through a uniform absorber. Attenuation includes photons removed by scattering as well as absorption. Its coefficient depends on energy and material; it is not a universal percentage per centimetre. Neutrons interact chiefly with nuclei rather than by direct electric ionisation.

steps.title: Work a time example
steps.body: An 800 Bq sample with a 2-hour half-life has expected activity 100 Bq after 6 hours: three half-lives leave one eighth. This does not mean every original nucleus survived exactly two hours. A detector count rate also depends on efficiency, geometry and background.

question.prompt: After three half-lives, what fraction of the original activity remains for one radionuclide?

options.reason: Exponential decay approaches zero statistically rather than stopping after three half-lives.
Three successive factors of one half give one eighth.
Half-life changes are multiplicative, not a division by elapsed count.

recall.prompt: Explain decay law and radiation interactions with matter: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: Three successive factors of one half give one eighth. Compton scattering redistributes energy between a lower-energy photon and an electron. An 800 Bq sample with a 2-hour half-life has expected activity 100 Bq after 6 hours: three half-lives leave one eighth. This does not mean every original nucleus survived exactly two hours. A detector count rate also depends on efficiency, geometry and background.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Detectors, count statistics and pulse spectra
lessons.summary: Follow a radiation event through conversion, amplification and discrimination.
lessons.section: Medical Biophysics I, topic 15; combined theory prompts 129–134

steps.title: Convert an event
steps.body: A scintillator converts some deposited energy into light. A photomultiplier converts that light into photoelectrons and amplifies their number through dynodes. Pulse height can track deposited energy under calibrated conditions; pulse count tracks detected events. Neither is automatically equal to source activity.

steps.title: Compare gas detectors
steps.body: An ionisation chamber collects primary ionisation charge. A proportional counter uses gas multiplication while retaining information about initial ionisation. In a Geiger–Müller tube, avalanches make pulse sizes largely independent of incident energy, so it is useful for counting but not ordinary pulse-height energy spectroscopy.

steps.title: Use semiconductor detectors
steps.body: Energy deposition creates electron–hole pairs that can be collected as charge. Detector material, thickness, noise and energy resolution affect performance. A discriminator rejects pulses below a threshold, reducing some noise but potentially rejecting genuine events. Calibration is needed to associate a channel number with an energy.

steps.title: Interpret counts statistically
steps.body: For independent Poisson events, the standard deviation of N counts is approximately √N. Relative counting uncertainty is about 1/√N. Background subtraction introduces uncertainty from both measurements. Dead time causes missed events at high rates, so observed counts need not rise linearly without limit.

steps.title: Work precision and gain
steps.body: Collecting 10,000 counts gives about 1% counting uncertainty before other errors, compared with 10% for 100 counts. Eight ideal dynodes each multiplying electrons by 3 give gain 3⁸ = 6561. Gain increases pulse amplitude, not the number of radioactive decays occurring in the sample.

question.prompt: To halve relative Poisson counting uncertainty, how many counts are needed?

options.reason: Relative uncertainty decreases with the square root of count number.
Fewer counts increase relative uncertainty.
1/√N halves when N increases fourfold.

recall.prompt: Explain detectors, count statistics and pulse spectra: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: 1/√N halves when N increases fourfold. Geiger avalanches largely remove the dependence of pulse size on initial ionisation. Collecting 10,000 counts gives about 1% counting uncertainty before other errors, compared with 10% for 100 counts. Eight ideal dynodes each multiplying electrons by 3 give gain 3⁸ = 6561. Gain increases pulse amplitude, not the number of radioactive decays occurring in the sample.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Absorbed dose, biological weighting and protection
lessons.summary: Keep activity, deposited energy and protection quantities separate.
lessons.section: Medical Biophysics I, topic 16; combined theory prompts 135–147

steps.title: Separate units
steps.body: Activity in Bq counts decays per second; absorbed dose D in gray is energy deposited per mass, with 1 Gy = 1 J/kg. Exposure is a charge-per-mass quantity defined for photon ionisation in air, not a general tissue dose. No universal Bq-to-Gy conversion exists without geometry, energies, time and biokinetics.

steps.title: Explain weighting
steps.body: Equivalent dose weights organ absorbed dose for radiation type. Effective dose additionally combines tissue-weighted contributions as a protection quantity. Both use sieverts, but identical units do not make them interchangeable with gray or with an individual patient's predicted injury. Weighting factors belong to a specified protection framework.

steps.title: Follow damage pathways
steps.body: Radiation can affect a target directly or indirectly through chemical species produced in surrounding material, notably water. Physical interactions precede chemical and biological responses. Tissue reactions and stochastic effects have different dose–response concepts. A dose number alone omits distribution, dose rate and biological context.

steps.title: Use protection principles
steps.body: Justification asks whether an exposure is warranted; optimisation seeks an appropriate balance while limiting unnecessary exposure. Time, distance and suitable shielding alter exposure pathways. Dose limits in regulated exposure categories are not interchangeable with patient medical exposures, and current local requirements must be checked separately.

steps.title: Work energy per mass
steps.body: If 0.02 J is deposited uniformly in 0.10 kg, absorbed dose is 0.20 Gy. Without radiation type and distribution this result cannot be relabelled as effective dose. Doubling mass at the same deposited energy halves absorbed dose; doubling activity alone does not determine the dose change.

question.prompt: 0.06 J is deposited in 0.30 kg. What is absorbed dose?

options.reason: Dose divides energy by mass rather than multiplying.
Becquerels measure decay rate, not deposited energy per mass.

recall.prompt: Explain absorbed dose, biological weighting and protection: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: D = 0.06/0.30 = 0.20 J/kg = 0.20 Gy. Activity alone does not specify energy deposition or tissue weighting. If 0.02 J is deposited uniformly in 0.10 kg, absorbed dose is 0.20 Gy. Without radiation type and distribution this result cannot be relabelled as effective dose. Doubling mass at the same deposited energy halves absorbed dose; doubling activity alone does not determine the dose change.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Tracers, biological clearance and effective half-life
lessons.summary: Choose a diagnostic tracer conceptually and distinguish physical decay from movement through the body.
lessons.section: Medical Biophysics I, topic 17; combined theory prompts 148–154

steps.title: Follow the labelled molecule
steps.body: A radiopharmaceutical combines a radionuclide with a chemical form that determines distribution. A detected signal can report uptake, transport or clearance, depending on the tracer and timing. Nuclear half-life is a property of the radionuclide; biological behaviour depends on chemistry and the system being observed.

steps.title: Match the measurement
steps.body: A useful tracer must provide emissions that the intended detector can measure, with suitable energy and timing. Chemical targeting, image contrast, radiation burden and practical supply all matter. An arbitrarily long half-life is not automatically useful, and choosing photon energy independently of detector and attenuation is incomplete.

steps.title: Combine removal processes
steps.body: When physical decay and biological elimination are independent first-order processes, λeff = λphys + λbio. Therefore 1/Teff = 1/Tphys + 1/Tbio. Effective half-life is shorter than either component. Real uptake and clearance can be multicompartmental, so one exponential may be only an approximation.

steps.title: Explain generators and curves
steps.body: A parent–daughter generator allows chemical separation of a useful daughter radionuclide, as in technetium-99m supply from molybdenum-99. An uptake curve combines delivery, accumulation, elimination and decay. Correcting for physical decay is necessary before treating the remaining curve as purely biological.

steps.title: Work the combination
steps.body: With a physical half-life of 6 hours and a biological half-life of 3 hours, 1/Teff = 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/2, giving 2 hours. Adding the half-lives to obtain 9 hours reverses the effect: two independent removal routes empty the pool faster.

question.prompt: Physical half-life is 8 h and biological half-life is 8 h under independent first-order removal. Effective half-life is…

options.reason: Two active loss processes remove material faster than either alone.
Independent loss rates add; half-lives do not.

recall.prompt: Explain tracers, biological clearance and effective half-life: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: 1/Teff = 1/8 + 1/8 = 1/4 h⁻¹. The labelled chemical form and biological handling govern distribution. With a physical half-life of 6 hours and a biological half-life of 3 hours, 1/Teff = 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/2, giving 2 hours. Adding the half-lives to obtain 9 hours reverses the effect: two independent removal routes empty the pool faster.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Gamma cameras, SPECT, PET and radiotherapy geometry
lessons.summary: Compare information pathways in nuclear imaging and explain spatial dose targeting.
lessons.section: Medical Biophysics I, topic 18; combined theory prompts 155–164

steps.title: Localise single photons
steps.body: A gamma camera uses a collimator to restrict photon directions, a detector to register events and electronics to estimate position and energy. Collimation improves spatial information but rejects many photons. A planar image combines depth information in projection; rotating views support SPECT reconstruction.

steps.title: Localise annihilation events
steps.body: PET detects near-coincident photons from positron annihilation and assigns a line of response between detectors. Many such events support reconstruction. Positron range, non-collinearity, scatter and random coincidences affect resolution and accuracy. PET measures a tracer distribution, not a direct photograph of every metabolic reaction.

steps.title: Combine modalities
steps.body: PET/CT and SPECT/CT combine functional tracer information with anatomical localisation and attenuation correction. Registration errors can arise from motion or mismatched acquisition conditions. Hybrid imaging does not remove the distinct limitations of each component; the physical origin of each image should remain clear.

steps.title: Shape therapeutic dose
steps.body: External-beam therapy directs radiation from outside; brachytherapy places sources near or within a treatment region. Multiple beam directions and collimation can concentrate dose geometrically. Charged-particle range and photon depth-dose behaviour differ. Planning must balance target coverage and surrounding tissues rather than assuming one beam only affects its target.

steps.title: Reason about sensitivity
steps.body: Narrower collimator acceptance commonly improves directional selection while reducing detected counts. More counts can improve statistical precision but are not equivalent to better intrinsic spatial resolution. Draw a line of response for PET and a collimated ray for a gamma camera to explain why their localisation mechanisms differ.

question.prompt: What provides a PET line of response?

options.text: One visible fluorescence photon in the skin
options.reason: PET does not localise events using skin fluorescence.
An acoustic echo belongs to ultrasound imaging.

options.text: Two near-coincident annihilation photons registered by opposing detectors
options.reason: Coincidence detection links an event to the line joining the detector pair.

recall.prompt: Explain gamma cameras, spect, pet and radiotherapy geometry: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: Coincidence detection links an event to the line joining the detector pair. Improved directional restriction commonly costs detected counts. Narrower collimator acceptance commonly improves directional selection while reducing detected counts. More counts can improve statistical precision but are not equivalent to better intrinsic spatial resolution.
