lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Biological signals, filtering and digitisation
lessons.summary: Trace a physiological signal from a transducer to a sampled record.
lessons.section: Medical Biophysics I, topic 19; combined theory prompts 165–173

steps.title: Classify the information
steps.body: Signals may be continuous or discrete in time, analogue or quantised in amplitude, periodic or aperiodic. A biological process must first be converted into a measurable quantity by a transducer. Distinguish the original signal from the displayed trace, which has already passed through sensors and processing.

steps.title: Read time and frequency
steps.body: Amplitude describes size; frequency describes repetition rate. Fourier analysis represents suitable signals as combinations of frequency components. A short pulse contains a broad frequency range. Changing a waveform's shape can therefore change its spectrum even when the main repetition period is unchanged.

steps.title: Explain filtering and amplification
steps.body: Low-pass filters attenuate higher frequencies; high-pass filters attenuate lower ones; band-pass filters select a range. Amplification scales signals but also acts on noise within its bandwidth. Filtering can remove interference and also distort meaningful features, so cutoffs must relate to the physiological question.

steps.title: Sample without inventing detail
steps.body: For a band-limited signal, the sampling rate must exceed twice the highest frequency to avoid aliasing under ideal reconstruction assumptions. An analogue anti-alias filter acts before sampling. Quantisation maps amplitudes into discrete levels; more bits reduce the step size for a fixed range but do not cure sensor noise.

steps.title: Work a sampling choice
steps.body: A signal restricted below 100 Hz needs a sampling rate above 200 samples/s, with practical margin for real filters. Sampling at 150 samples/s can misrepresent high-frequency content as lower-frequency variation. Upsampling that record later cannot recover information already aliased at acquisition.

question.prompt: Where should an anti-alias filter act?

options.reason: Bandwidth must be limited before sampling creates frequency ambiguity.

options.text: Only after displaying the aliased signal
options.reason: Filtering after aliasing cannot identify which folded frequencies were originally present.
Power filtering is not the required signal bandwidth restriction.

recall.prompt: Explain biological signals, filtering and digitisation: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: Bandwidth must be limited before sampling creates frequency ambiguity. 250 samples/s exceeds 160 samples/s; real systems also need appropriate filtering. A signal restricted below 100 Hz needs a sampling rate above 200 samples/s, with practical margin for real filters. Sampling at 150 samples/s can misrepresent high-frequency content as lower-frequency variation. Upsampling that record later cannot recover information already aliased at acquisition.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: X-ray tubes, spectra and beam quality
lessons.summary: Separate tube voltage, current and target material when predicting an X-ray spectrum.
lessons.section: Biophysics II, topic 20; combined theory prompts 174–179

steps.title: Follow the electrons
steps.body: A heated cathode supplies electrons that accelerate toward an anode through a potential difference. Their maximum kinetic energy is eV. Most deposited energy becomes heat; only a fraction becomes X-rays. Target design and cooling manage this energy load rather than implying perfect conversion into useful photons.

steps.title: Explain two spectral components
steps.body: Bremsstrahlung results from electron deceleration and produces a continuum up to a maximum photon energy. Characteristic lines arise when inner-shell vacancies are filled, with energies determined by the target element's atomic levels. Raising current increases electron delivery; it does not change those characteristic transition energies.

steps.title: Relate voltage and wavelength
steps.body: The short-wavelength cutoff follows λmin = hc/(eV), the Duane–Hunt relation. Increasing tube voltage raises the maximum photon energy and generally changes the spectrum and output. It is incorrect to describe every emitted photon as having the maximum energy, because the spectrum contains a range.

steps.title: Explain filtration and attenuation
steps.body: Added filtration preferentially removes lower-energy photons and hardens the beam. Attenuation depends on material composition, thickness and photon energy, with both photoelectric and Compton contributions. A beam's effective attenuation can change with depth as its spectral composition changes.

steps.title: Work a cutoff
steps.body: At 50 kV, maximum photon energy is 50 keV. Using hc ≈ 1.240 keV·nm gives λmin ≈ 0.0248 nm. Doubling tube current at the same voltage chiefly raises photon output under otherwise fixed conditions; it does not halve this cutoff wavelength.

question.prompt: A tube voltage of 80 kV sets a maximum photon energy of…

options.reason: The spectrum includes lower energies as well.
Maximum photon energy equals the maximum electron energy eV.
An electron accelerated through 80,000 V gains 80,000 eV.

recall.prompt: Explain x-ray tubes, spectra and beam quality: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: Maximum photon energy equals the maximum electron energy eV. More electrons strike the target per second, increasing output in the usual model. At 50 kV, maximum photon energy is 50 keV. Using hc ≈ 1.240 keV·nm gives λmin ≈ 0.0248 nm. Doubling tube current at the same voltage chiefly raises photon output under otherwise fixed conditions; it does not halve this cutoff wavelength.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Projection radiography, CT reconstruction and windowing
lessons.summary: Understand why a projection is ambiguous and how CT estimates a cross-section.
lessons.section: Biophysics II, topic 21; combined theory prompts 180–187

steps.title: Read a projection
steps.body: A radiograph records transmitted X-rays after passage through many structures along each path. Stronger attenuation reduces detector exposure along that line. Different arrangements can produce the same integrated attenuation, so a single projection cannot uniquely reveal depth or separate overlapping structures.

steps.title: Build a tomographic idea
steps.body: CT acquires many angular projections and reconstructs spatial attenuation estimates. A simple sum of backprojected rays blurs the image; filtered or iterative methods address the reconstruction problem. Patient motion, scatter, beam hardening and incomplete data can introduce artifacts despite a visually sharp display.

steps.title: Define the CT scale
steps.body: Hounsfield units are defined approximately as HU = 1000(μtissue − μwater)/μwater under the measurement conditions. Water is near 0 HU and air near −1000 HU. Values depend on composition, energy and acquisition; a tissue name does not guarantee a single universal HU value.

steps.title: Separate display from measurement
steps.body: Window width sets the displayed attenuation range and window level its centre. Narrow windows improve visibility of small differences within that interval but clip values outside it. Adjusting a window changes how existing data appear; it does not acquire missing spatial detail or remove a physical artifact.

steps.title: Work a relative attenuation
steps.body: If a reconstructed material has μ = 1.2 μwater, its value is 200 HU. Two differently placed absorbers with the same summed line attenuation may look identical in one projection but differ across other viewing angles. Explain the value of rotation using that ambiguity before memorising scanner component names.

question.prompt: A material has attenuation coefficient 1.5 times water. Its CT value is…

options.reason: The HU definition subtracts the water reference before multiplying.
Attenuation above water produces a positive value.

recall.prompt: Explain projection radiography, ct reconstruction and windowing: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: 1000(1.5 − 1) = 500 HU. Windowing remaps the existing reconstructed values to a visible range. If a reconstructed material has μ = 1.2 μwater, its value is 200 HU. Two differently placed absorbers with the same summed line attenuation may look identical in one projection but differ across other viewing angles. Explain the value of rotation using that ambiguity before memorising scanner component names.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Continuity, viscosity and resistance to flow
lessons.summary: Predict flow changes while stating when ideal fluid and tube models apply.
lessons.section: Biophysics II, topic 22; combined theory prompts 188–196

steps.title: Conserve volume
steps.body: For steady incompressible flow, Q = Av and the same volume flow passes successive cross-sections without leaks. A smaller total area therefore means greater mean speed at fixed Q. In a branching network, use the sum of parallel cross-sectional areas rather than comparing only one small vessel with one large vessel.

steps.title: Distinguish ideal and viscous descriptions
steps.body: Bernoulli's equation relates pressure, speed and height along an ideal steady streamline without dissipative losses. Real viscous flow loses mechanical energy. Newtonian shear stress obeys τ = η dv/dy. Blood's apparent viscosity depends on flow conditions and cellular content, so it is not a universal constant.

steps.title: Use Poiseuille's law
steps.body: For steady fully developed laminar flow of a Newtonian fluid in a rigid circular tube, Q = πr⁴Δp/(8ηL). Resistance is 8ηL/(πr⁴). Radius has a strong fourth-power effect. Pulsatile blood vessels with flexible walls and non-Newtonian behaviour depart from this exact model.

steps.title: Compare regimes and drag
steps.body: Reynolds number Re = ρvD/η compares inertial and viscous tendencies; geometry and disturbances affect transition. Stokes drag F = 6πηrv applies to a small sphere at low Reynolds number. Plasma skimming and cell distribution at branches can change local blood composition as well as flow.

steps.title: Work a radius change
steps.body: At fixed pressure difference, length and viscosity, doubling radius predicts 16 times the flow. At fixed flow, the same change reduces the required pressure difference to one sixteenth. These are different experimental constraints; always state what is held constant.

question.prompt: Tube radius halves under Poiseuille assumptions with fixed pressure difference. Flow becomes…

options.reason: (1/2)⁴ = 1/16 at fixed driving pressure.
The radius enters as the fourth power.
Narrowing increases resistance and reduces flow.

recall.prompt: Explain continuity, viscosity and resistance to flow: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: (1/2)⁴ = 1/16 at fixed driving pressure. Mean network speed reflects total area, not one capillary's diameter. At fixed pressure difference, length and viscosity, doubling radius predicts 16 times the flow. At fixed flow, the same change reduces the required pressure difference to one sixteenth. These are different experimental constraints; always state what is held constant.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Diffusion, osmosis and heat transport
lessons.summary: Connect gradients, random motion and the time needed to cross a distance.
lessons.section: Biophysics II, topic 23; combined theory prompts 197–206

steps.title: Start from random motion
steps.body: Brownian motion is irregular motion driven by molecular impacts. Net diffusion emerges statistically from concentration differences, not from molecules intentionally seeking dilute regions. Fick's first law J = −D dc/dx expresses flux down a gradient, with the minus sign indicating direction.

steps.title: Follow time dependence
steps.body: Fick's second law describes how concentration changes as diffusion redistributes material. In one dimension, mean squared displacement is 2Dt for free diffusion. Typical diffusion time therefore grows with distance squared. Diffusion is effective over short cellular distances but rapidly becomes slow across much larger distances.

steps.title: Relate size and transport
steps.body: For a sphere in a suitable dilute fluid, Stokes–Einstein gives D = kBT/(6πηr). Higher temperature tends to increase D, while greater viscosity or particle radius reduces it in this model. Binding, crowding and membranes can make transport in tissue differ from free diffusion.

steps.title: Explain osmotic and thermal driving
steps.body: Osmosis is solvent movement associated with a chemical-potential difference across a selectively permeable boundary. For ideal dilute solutions, osmotic pressure is approximately cRT for solute particle concentration c. Fourier's heat law has a similar gradient form, with heat flux proportional to negative temperature gradient; thermodiffusion couples temperature and material transport.

steps.title: Work a distance comparison
steps.body: If diffusion across 10 μm takes a characteristic time t, crossing 100 μm under the same conditions takes roughly 100t. In alveolar exchange, area, barrier thickness and partial-pressure gradients influence transfer. Convection brings gases to the exchange surface; diffusion carries them across the thin barrier.

question.prompt: A diffusion distance triples while D stays fixed. Characteristic time changes by…

options.reason: Longer diffusion distance increases, not decreases, the time.
t scales as L²/D, so 3² gives a factor of nine.
Diffusion time scales with squared distance.

recall.prompt: Explain diffusion, osmosis and heat transport: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: t scales as L²/D, so 3² gives a factor of nine. Unequal numbers available to cross create a net flux while individual motion remains random. If diffusion across 10 μm takes a characteristic time t, crossing 100 μm under the same conditions takes roughly 100t. In alveolar exchange, area, barrier thickness and partial-pressure gradients influence transfer. Convection brings gases to the exchange surface; diffusion carries them across the thin barrier.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Thermodynamic systems and the first law
lessons.summary: Account for energy transfers without confusing heat, work and stored energy.
lessons.section: Biophysics II, topic 24; combined theory prompts 207–210, 213, 216

steps.title: Choose the boundary
steps.body: An open system exchanges matter and energy; a closed system exchanges energy but not matter; an isolated system exchanges neither. The boundary determines which flows must be counted. A living organism is typically open, while a sealed but heated container is closed rather than isolated.

steps.title: Distinguish state and transfer
steps.body: Internal energy is a state property incorporating microscopic contributions. Heat and work describe energy transfer processes, not substances stored separately inside an object. Temperature is an intensive state variable and is not the total thermal energy. Extensive quantities such as mass and total energy scale with system size.

steps.title: State the sign convention
steps.body: Using work W done by the system, the first law for a closed system is ΔU = Q − W. Expansion against external pressure transfers work outward. With the alternative convention of work done on the system, the sign changes. Neither convention is wrong if it is explicitly and consistently used.

steps.title: Compare processes
steps.body: Isochoric means constant volume, isobaric constant pressure, isothermal constant temperature and adiabatic no heat transfer. An isothermal process need not be isolated or adiabatic. For an ideal gas, internal energy depends on temperature, so isothermal expansion can require heat input to balance work output.

steps.title: Work an energy balance
steps.body: A closed system absorbs 150 J of heat and performs 40 J of work on its surroundings. Its internal energy rises by 110 J. If the same system instead has 40 J of work done on it, the increase is 190 J. A diagram of boundary arrows prevents most sign errors.

question.prompt: A system receives 100 J of heat and does 30 J of work. ΔU is…

options.reason: Work done by the system leaves it under this sign convention.
More energy enters as heat than leaves as work.

recall.prompt: Explain thermodynamic systems and the first law: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: ΔU = Q − W = 100 − 30 = 70 J. The boundary permits energy transfer but prevents matter exchange. A closed system absorbs 150 J of heat and performs 40 J of work on its surroundings. Its internal energy rises by 110 J. If the same system instead has 40 J of work done on it, the increase is 190 J. A diagram of boundary arrows prevents most sign errors.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Entropy, free energy and equilibrium
lessons.summary: Choose the correct thermodynamic criterion for the constraints of a biological process.
lessons.section: Biophysics II, topic 25; combined theory prompts 211–212, 214–215, 217–218

steps.title: Interpret the second law
steps.body: For an isolated system, total entropy cannot decrease in a spontaneous process. A subsystem can become more ordered while exporting heat or matter, so local order does not violate the second law. Biological organisation requires an energy and entropy balance with the surroundings rather than a claim that organisms escape thermodynamics.

steps.title: Connect microscopic and macroscopic views
steps.body: Boltzmann entropy S = kB ln Ω links multiplicity with entropy for an appropriate statistical description. For a reversible heat transfer, dS = δQrev/T. Irreversible processes generate entropy. The third law concerns entropy as temperature approaches absolute zero under specified conditions; it does not say ordinary biological entropy is zero.

steps.title: Choose a potential
steps.body: Helmholtz free energy F = U − TS is useful at fixed temperature and volume. Gibbs free energy G = H − TS, with H = U + pV, is useful at fixed temperature and pressure. Under appropriate closed-system constraints, spontaneous change lowers the relevant potential toward equilibrium.

steps.title: Separate favourability and rate
steps.body: A negative reaction ΔG indicates thermodynamic favourability in the specified state, not a fast reaction. Activation barriers determine kinetics. Concentrations affect ΔG through chemical potentials, so a standard free-energy value alone does not specify the direction under every cellular condition. Coupling can make a combined process favourable.

steps.title: Work a balance
steps.body: At fixed temperature and pressure, let ΔH = 20 kJ/mol and TΔS = 30 kJ/mol. Then ΔG = −10 kJ/mol, despite positive enthalpy change. If the entropy contribution changes with conditions, the result may differ. State units consistently and do not multiply a Celsius value into TΔS.

question.prompt: At fixed T and p, ΔH = 10 kJ/mol and TΔS = 15 kJ/mol. ΔG is…

options.reason: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS = −5 kJ/mol.
Gibbs change subtracts the entropy contribution.
10 minus 15 is negative.

recall.prompt: Explain entropy, free energy and equilibrium: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS = −5 kJ/mol. Kinetics and thermodynamic driving force answer different questions. At fixed temperature and pressure, let ΔH = 20 kJ/mol and TΔS = 30 kJ/mol. Then ΔG = −10 kJ/mol, despite positive enthalpy change. If the entropy contribution changes with conditions, the result may differ. State units consistently and do not multiply a Celsius value into TΔS.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Membrane potentials, permeability and the RC model
lessons.summary: Connect ion gradients to voltage and explain passive charging and spread.
lessons.section: Biophysics II, topic 26; combined theory prompts 219–226

steps.title: Build an electrochemical balance
steps.body: An ion moves under both concentration and electrical influences. For one permeant ion at equilibrium, the Nernst equation gives E = RT/(zF) ln(coutside/cinside) using inside potential relative to outside. The sign depends on valence as well as the concentration ratio. Equilibrium for one ion need not mean zero current for every ion.

steps.title: Use selective permeability
steps.body: The resting membrane potential reflects gradients and relative permeabilities. The Goldman–Hodgkin–Katz voltage equation extends the comparison to several permeant monovalent ions under its assumptions, with anion concentrations appearing in reversed positions. Pumps maintain gradients over time; the voltage is not simply a direct count of pump cycles.

steps.title: Model electrical storage
steps.body: A membrane separates charge and behaves capacitively, while conducting pathways provide resistance. An elementary RC model has time constant τ = RC. After one time constant, a charging response has completed about 63% of its final change. This does not mean ions have all reached their equilibrium distributions.

steps.title: Explain spatial spread and Donnan effects
steps.body: Passive voltage changes decay along a leaky cable; length constant describes the distance over which amplitude falls to 1/e in a simple model. Regenerative action potentials are different. Impermeant charged solutes can create Donnan ion distributions and osmotic effects, constrained in cells by pumps and volume regulation.

steps.title: Work a Nernst estimate
steps.body: For K⁺ at about 37°C with outside/inside concentration ratio 0.1, E is approximately −61.5 mV. Increasing outside K⁺ makes that equilibrium potential less negative. Predict the direction before calculating, and distinguish this single-ion value from a full resting-potential estimate.

question.prompt: At 37°C, a monovalent cation has outside/inside ratio 0.1. Its Nernst potential is approximately…

options.reason: The concentrations are unequal, so the equilibrium voltage is not zero.
The logarithm of 0.1 is negative for a positive ion.

recall.prompt: Explain membrane potentials, permeability and the rc model: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: E ≈ 61.5 log₁₀(0.1) mV = −61.5 mV. 1 − e⁻¹ ≈ 0.632 describes the completed charging fraction. For K⁺ at about 37°C with outside/inside concentration ratio 0.1, E is approximately −61.5 mV. Increasing outside K⁺ makes that equilibrium potential less negative. Predict the direction before calculating, and distinguish this single-ion value from a full resting-potential estimate.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Action potentials and impulse propagation
lessons.summary: Separate regenerative signalling from passive current spread.
lessons.section: Biophysics II, topic 27; combined theory prompts 227–231

steps.title: Start with positive feedback
steps.body: In a typical axon, sufficient depolarisation activates voltage-gated inward current, producing further depolarisation. Threshold marks a balance where regenerative activation can outpace opposing processes. The detailed channel types and waveform vary among excitable cells, so a neuronal sodium spike is not every action potential.

steps.title: Follow recovery
steps.body: Sodium-channel inactivation and delayed outward potassium current help repolarise a typical axon. Refractoriness reflects channel state and conductances: during an absolute refractory interval, another normal spike cannot be triggered; during a relative interval, excitability is reduced. It is not simply that all ions have been used up.

steps.title: Explain propagation
steps.body: Local circuit currents depolarise adjacent membrane, where new regenerative current develops. The passive current spreads with decrement, but a normal propagated action potential is repeatedly renewed rather than exponentially shrinking along the entire axon. Refractory membrane behind the front supports forward progression after initiation.

steps.title: Compare fibre properties
steps.body: Increasing diameter reduces internal resistance and can increase conduction speed. Myelin reduces current leakage and effective membrane charging requirements between nodes; regeneration occurs at nodes of Ranvier. Saltatory conduction does not mean ions leap through empty space from one node to the next.

steps.title: Connect to recording
steps.body: An intracellular voltage and a surface extracellular potential are different measurements. Surface signals depend on spatial current distributions, orientation and volume conduction. Stronger stimulation often changes recruitment or firing rate rather than increasing the height of each all-or-none spike in one healthy axon.

question.prompt: Why does a normal action potential maintain its size along an axon?

options.text: Passive voltage never decays with distance
options.reason: Passive cable signals do decay; regeneration is the crucial distinction.

options.text: Each electron travels the entire axon instantly
options.reason: Propagation is not instantaneous long-distance travel of one electron.

options.text: Local membrane currents regenerate the spike
options.reason: Adjacent excitable membrane renews the signal through voltage-dependent currents.

recall.prompt: Explain action potentials and impulse propagation: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: Adjacent excitable membrane renews the signal through voltage-dependent currents. Incomplete recovery and persisting conductances make excitation harder. An intracellular voltage and a surface extracellular potential are different measurements. Surface signals depend on spatial current distributions, orientation and volume conduction. Stronger stimulation often changes recruitment or firing rate rather than increasing the height of each all-or-none spike in one healthy axon.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Ultrasound echoes, Doppler shifts and energy deposition
lessons.summary: Link an acoustic measurement to depth or motion while recognising its assumptions.
lessons.section: Biophysics II, topic 28; combined theory prompts 232–240

steps.title: Generate and receive sound
steps.body: A piezoelectric transducer converts electrical drive into mechanical vibration and returning pressure variations into an electrical signal. Ultrasound is a mechanical wave above the usual audible frequency range. Its speed depends on the medium; diagnostic calculations often use an approximate soft-tissue speed rather than a universal value.

steps.title: Explain interfaces
steps.body: Acoustic impedance Z = ρc influences reflection. At normal incidence between ideal media, intensity reflection coefficient is ((Z₂ − Z₁)/(Z₂ + Z₁))². A large air–tissue mismatch impedes transmission, which is why coupling matters. Attenuation and scattering also reduce returning signals with depth.

steps.title: Use pulse timing and display modes
steps.body: For a pulse returning after time t, reflector depth is d = ct/2 because travel is outward and back. A-mode displays amplitude along a line; B-mode maps brightness; M-mode tracks a selected line over time. Finite pulse length and beam width constrain resolution.

steps.title: Interpret Doppler and therapy
steps.body: For backscattered sound at small flow speed, Δf ≈ 2f₀v cos θ/c. Angle uncertainty therefore affects inferred velocity. Therapeutic ultrasound uses acoustic energy deposition and mechanical effects; absence of ionising radiation does not imply absence of biological effects.

steps.title: Work an echo
steps.body: With c = 1540 m/s and return time 100 μs, depth is 0.077 m, or 7.7 cm. Omitting the factor of two doubles the estimate. Higher frequency can improve detail but often increases attenuation, creating a resolution–penetration tradeoff.

question.prompt: At c = 1540 m/s, a 40 μs echo return corresponds to depth…

options.reason: The total path is twice the reflector depth.
Convert metres to centimetres after applying the round-trip factor.

recall.prompt: Explain ultrasound echoes, doppler shifts and energy deposition: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: 1540 × 40 × 10⁻⁶ / 2 = 0.0308 m = 3.08 cm. Only the velocity component along the beam contributes in this model. With c = 1540 m/s and return time 100 μs, depth is 0.077 m, or 7.7 cm. Omitting the factor of two doubles the estimate. Higher frequency can improve detail but often increases attenuation, creating a resolution–penetration tradeoff.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Water, protein folding and polymer elasticity
lessons.summary: Explain how solvent and molecular flexibility shape biological material behaviour.
lessons.section: Biophysics II, topic 29; combined theory prompts 241–249

steps.title: Connect water structure to properties
steps.body: Water's polar molecules form a dynamic hydrogen-bond network. Its phase behaviour and unusual density change on freezing reflect molecular arrangement, not permanent rigid bonds between all molecules. High heat capacity helps buffer temperature changes; phase diagrams specify pressure and temperature rather than one universal boiling point.

steps.title: Organise macromolecular structure
steps.body: Protein primary structure is sequence; secondary structures organise local backbone patterns; tertiary and quaternary structures describe larger folding and assembly. Hydrogen bonding, electrostatic interactions, dispersion, covalent links and solvent effects contribute. DNA and polysaccharides have different repeating units and structural constraints.

steps.title: Explain folding energetics
steps.body: Folding balances intramolecular contacts, solvent effects and conformational entropy. Many sequences have a preferred native ensemble under particular conditions, but misfolding and kinetic trapping can occur. A favourable free-energy difference does not guarantee rapid folding without barriers or assistance.

steps.title: Distinguish elastic mechanisms
steps.body: Stretching a flexible polymer initially restricts available conformations, producing an entropic restoring tendency. At greater extension, bond-angle and bond-stretching energies become more important. Persistence length quantifies bending stiffness in a chain model. A polymer is not an indefinitely extensible ideal spring.

steps.title: Interpret a force–extension curve
steps.body: A chain can become much harder to extend near its contour length even without adding new crosslinks. Double-stranded DNA combines bending flexibility at larger scales with molecular stiffness at shorter scales. State the length scale, solvent and force regime before assigning one universal elastic constant.

question.prompt: Why can stretching a flexible polymer create a restoring force?

options.text: The polymer creates energy without input
options.reason: Work must be supplied to constrain the chain.
Reducing conformational entropy can produce an entropic restoring force.

options.text: Every covalent bond must immediately break
options.reason: Entropic elasticity occurs without breaking every bond.

recall.prompt: Explain water, protein folding and polymer elasticity: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: Reducing conformational entropy can produce an entropic restoring force. Primary structure identifies the linear sequence of residues. A chain can become much harder to extend near its contour length even without adding new crosslinks. Double-stranded DNA combines bending flexibility at larger scales with molecular stiffness at shorter scales. State the length scale, solvent and force regime before assigning one universal elastic constant.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Vision, hearing and sensory coding
lessons.summary: Connect stimulus energy to receptor responses and perceived intensity.
lessons.section: Biophysics II, topic 30; combined theory prompts 250–265

steps.title: Separate transduction from perception
steps.body: Receptors convert a stimulus into a graded electrical response; downstream spike rate, timing and population activity can encode information. Adaptation changes response during sustained stimulation. Equal physical changes need not produce equal perceptual changes, and a receptor potential is not itself an all-or-none axonal spike.

steps.title: Compare psychophysical laws
steps.body: Weber–Fechner relates sensation approximately to a logarithm of stimulus intensity over suitable ranges. Stevens's power law uses a modality-dependent exponent. These are empirical descriptions with domains of usefulness. Absolute threshold and difference threshold ask different questions, so one number cannot describe the entire sensory system.

steps.title: Trace hearing
steps.body: The outer ear guides sound; the middle ear improves energy transfer toward cochlear fluids. Travelling waves along the basilar membrane create place-dependent frequency sensitivity. Hair-cell bundle displacement changes transduction currents; outer hair cells contribute active mechanical amplification. Sound level in decibels is not identical to subjective loudness.

steps.title: Trace vision
steps.body: Phototransduction alters photoreceptor membrane currents after photon absorption. Rods support sensitive low-light vision; cones support colour and high-acuity vision under suitable illumination. Colour depends on comparing receptor signals rather than assigning one wavelength to every perceived colour. The optic-disc blind spot lacks photoreceptors.

steps.title: Compare loudness scales
steps.body: Phon is a loudness level defined by comparison with a 1 kHz reference tone. Sone expresses relative loudness; the conventional reference is 1 sone at 40 phon. Equal decibel levels at different frequencies need not sound equally loud. Describe frequency and reference conditions when interpreting an audiogram.

question.prompt: What is a receptor potential?

options.reason: Receptor potentials are generally graded rather than identical axonal spikes.

options.text: The external stimulus intensity in watts
options.reason: It is an electrical response, not the stimulus's power.

options.text: A graded response associated with stimulus transduction
options.reason: Transduction creates a graded electrical signal that can influence later neural firing.

recall.prompt: Explain vision, hearing and sensory coding: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: Transduction creates a graded electrical signal that can influence later neural firing. Equal physical level is not equivalent to equal perceived loudness. Phon is a loudness level defined by comparison with a 1 kHz reference tone. Sone expresses relative loudness; the conventional reference is 1 sone at 40 phon. Equal decibel levels at different frequencies need not sound equally loud. Describe frequency and reference conditions when interpreting an audiogram.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Stress, strain and viscoelastic tissues
lessons.summary: Distinguish material stiffness from geometry and time-dependent response.
lessons.section: Biophysics II, topic 31; combined theory prompts 266–272

steps.title: Normalise force and deformation
steps.body: Stress is force per area, measured in pascals. Strain is relative deformation and is dimensionless. In a linear uniaxial elastic regime, stress = E × strain, where E is Young's modulus. A sample's overall stiffness also depends on its length and cross-sectional area.

steps.title: Compare elastic and viscous elements
steps.body: An ideal spring responds elastically; a dashpot represents rate-dependent viscous response. Maxwell and Kelvin–Voigt arrangements combine these elements differently. Biological tissues often show creep, stress relaxation and hysteresis, so one instantaneous modulus cannot capture every loading protocol.

steps.title: Explain time-dependent behaviour
steps.body: Under fixed strain, stress relaxation is a decline in required stress over time. Under fixed stress, creep is increasing strain. Hysteresis means loading and unloading follow different paths, with loop area representing dissipated energy. These are experimentally distinguishable behaviours, not interchangeable labels.

steps.title: Apply geometry to walls
steps.body: Thin-wall Laplace approximations link transmural pressure, radius and wall stress. For a cylinder, circumferential stress is approximately Pr/h; for a sphere it is Pr/(2h). Shape and thin-wall assumptions matter. Larger radius at fixed pressure and thickness increases the required wall stress.

steps.title: Connect tissue architecture
steps.body: Bone and enamel combine mineral and organic structure, giving different stiffness and toughness profiles. Arteries show nonlinear elastic and viscoelastic responses as structural fibres are recruited. For stress 2 MPa and strain 0.01 in a linear test, E = 200 MPa; changing sample geometry alone does not redefine that material modulus.

question.prompt: At constant strain, measured stress falls with time. This is…

options.reason: Stress relaxation is a time-dependent decrease in stress at fixed deformation.
Creep uses a fixed stress and observes changing strain.

options.text: A definition of perfectly elastic behaviour
options.reason: A perfectly elastic spring would maintain stress at fixed strain.

recall.prompt: Explain stress, strain and viscoelastic tissues: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: Stress relaxation is a time-dependent decrease in stress at fixed deformation. The thin-cylinder expression σ ≈ Pr/h predicts a twofold increase. Bone and enamel combine mineral and organic structure, giving different stiffness and toughness profiles. Arteries show nonlinear elastic and viscoelastic responses as structural fibres are recruited. For stress 2 MPa and strain 0.01 in a linear test, E = 200 MPa; changing sample geometry alone does not redefine that material modulus.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Muscle mechanics and molecular motors
lessons.summary: Relate ATP-driven cycles to force, movement and external work.
lessons.section: Biophysics II, topic 32; combined theory prompts 273–277, 279–280

steps.title: Identify motor functions
steps.body: Myosin, kinesin and dynein convert chemical free energy into coordinated mechanical steps. Processivity describes how many steps a motor can take before detaching, not simply its maximum speed. Load, ATP availability and track properties influence motion. Thermal fluctuations coexist with directed molecular transport.

steps.title: Explain sliding filaments
steps.body: Muscle shortening arises from relative sliding of actin and myosin, not wholesale shortening of the filaments. Cross-bridge attachment, force generation and detachment form a cycle coupled to ATP chemistry. Calcium regulation makes suitable binding interactions available; ATP is also needed for detachment.

steps.title: Compare contraction conditions
steps.body: Isometric means fixed overall muscle length; isotonic describes an idealised constant-load condition. External mechanical work is force times displacement along the force direction, so a strictly isometric contraction performs no external shortening work despite consuming energy. Internal processes and heat production continue.

steps.title: Read force and timing
steps.body: Repeated activation can sum twitches and, in suitable muscle, produce tetanus. Force–velocity behaviour links shortening speed to load; maximum shortening speed is not the point of maximum power because power also requires force. Muscle length affects overlap and force-generating capacity.

steps.title: Work and interpret
steps.body: A constant 20 N force moving a load 0.05 m performs 1 J of work. At zero displacement external work is zero even if tension is 20 N. Compare this with energy consumed rather than equating mechanical output with every ATP molecule's free-energy change.

question.prompt: During a strictly isometric contraction, external shortening work is…

options.text: Equal to every joule of chemical energy used
options.reason: Chemical energy can become heat or support internal processes.
External work FΔx vanishes when overall shortening is zero.
Work also requires displacement along the force.

recall.prompt: Explain muscle mechanics and molecular motors: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: External work FΔx vanishes when overall shortening is zero. A processive motor remains attached through multiple successive steps. A constant 20 N force moving a load 0.05 m performs 1 J of work. At zero displacement external work is zero even if tension is 20 N.
