lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: X-ray diffraction and mass spectrometry
lessons.summary: Compare structural inference from diffraction with separation by mass-to-charge ratio.
lessons.section: Biophysics II, topic 33; combined theory prompts 278, 281–284

steps.title: Read a diffraction condition
steps.body: A periodic lattice scatters X-rays into directions that depend on spatial arrangement. Bragg's relation nλ = 2d sin θ links wavelength, plane spacing and angle. The measured pattern is not a magnified shadow of the molecule. Inferring structure requires reconstruction, including treatment of phase information.

steps.title: Connect crystal to model
steps.body: A crystal contains repeated units whose scattering adds coherently in selected directions. Data quality, resolution, disorder and model fitting affect the resulting molecular structure. A fitted atomic model is an interpretation constrained by measurements; flexible regions may be poorly represented or unresolved.

steps.title: Create ions for mass analysis
steps.body: Mass spectrometry measures ions according to mass-to-charge ratio, m/z. Electrospray and MALDI can introduce large biomolecules using different ionisation processes. Multiple charge states and fragmentation complicate direct conversion from peak position to molecular mass. Neutral molecules must first become measurable ions.

steps.title: Explain time of flight
steps.body: In a simplified time-of-flight analyser with the same accelerating potential, flight time scales as √(m/q) for the same path. A lighter or more highly charged ion arrives earlier under those conditions. The instrument requires calibration and controlled starting conditions, not just a stopwatch.

steps.title: Work a comparison
steps.body: Two ions with equal charge and a fourfold mass difference have flight times in a 2:1 ratio in the ideal model. In diffraction, increasing plane spacing at fixed wavelength lowers the first-order Bragg angle. State which experimental variable is fixed before making either prediction.

question.prompt: With equal charge and acceleration voltage, a fourfold ion mass gives what ideal flight-time factor?

options.reason: Flight time scales with the square root of mass-to-charge ratio.
A heavier ion at equal charge does not arrive faster in this model.
√4 = 2 for the same path and accelerating potential.

recall.prompt: Explain x-ray diffraction and mass spectrometry: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: √4 = 2 for the same path and accelerating potential. Ion separation is generally expressed as m/z, so charge state matters. Two ions with equal charge and a fourfold mass difference have flight times in a 2:1 ratio in the ideal model. In diffraction, increasing plane spacing at fixed wavelength lowers the first-order Bragg angle. State which experimental variable is fixed before making either prediction.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Spin, NMR, ESR and MRI contrast
lessons.summary: Connect resonance and relaxation to spatially encoded images.
lessons.section: Biophysics II, topic 34; combined theory prompts 285–293

steps.title: Introduce spin and resonance
steps.body: Particles with appropriate magnetic moments interact with an applied field. The Stern–Gerlach experiment illustrates quantised angular-momentum projections. NMR probes suitable nuclei, while ESR probes unpaired electron spins. Resonance frequency follows the Larmor relation ω₀ = γB₀, or f₀ = γB₀/(2π).

steps.title: Excite and detect
steps.body: A radiofrequency field near resonance perturbs net magnetisation. The subsequent changing transverse magnetisation induces a measurable signal. Chemical shielding shifts resonance slightly, producing chemical-shift information in spectroscopy. A resonance peak is not generated by physically spinning the entire sample at the radiofrequency.

steps.title: Separate relaxation times
steps.body: T1 describes longitudinal recovery toward equilibrium; T2 describes loss of transverse coherence from spin interactions. Field inhomogeneity adds dephasing captured by T2*, which is generally no longer than T2. These processes overlap in time but describe different magnetisation components.

steps.title: Encode location and contrast
steps.body: Magnetic-field gradients make resonance behaviour position dependent, supporting spatial encoding. Pulse sequence choices control contrast weighting, including sensitivity to relaxation and proton density. A bright region therefore depends on the sequence; brightness does not identify one tissue universally.

steps.title: Work a recovery example
steps.body: For ideal recovery from zero longitudinal magnetisation, Mz/M0 = 1 − exp(−t/T1). At t = T1, recovery is about 63%. Doubling the main field doubles Larmor frequency for the same nucleus. MRI uses no ionising photons for this signal, but magnetic and radiofrequency fields still require controlled use.

question.prompt: After one T1 from zero longitudinal magnetisation, ideal recovery is about…

options.reason: 1 − e⁻¹ gives approximately 63% recovery.
37% is the unrecovered fraction in this model.
Recovery is exponential and not complete at one time constant.

recall.prompt: Explain spin, nmr, esr and mri contrast: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: 1 − e⁻¹ gives approximately 63% recovery. Gradients make resonance phase and frequency vary with position. For ideal recovery from zero longitudinal magnetisation, Mz/M0 = 1 − exp(−t/T1). At t = T1, recovery is about 63%. Doubling the main field doubles Larmor frequency for the same nucleus. MRI uses no ionising photons for this signal, but magnetic and radiofrequency fields still require controlled use.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Circulation, cardiac work and the ECG
lessons.summary: Connect pressure, flow and electrical recordings without treating them as the same signal.
lessons.section: Biophysics II, topic 35; combined theory prompts 294–303

steps.title: Follow pressure and resistance
steps.body: Flow is driven by a pressure difference and limited by vascular resistance. Mean pressure falls along the systemic circuit, with major regulation in resistance vessels. A pressure value at one point does not by itself determine flow; the downstream pressure and resistance also matter.

steps.title: Explain the Windkessel effect
steps.body: Elastic large arteries store some energy during ejection and release it during diastole, smoothing flow. This compliance effect is distinct from active cardiac pumping. Total cross-sectional area changes through the network, so mean speed need not follow pressure with the same spatial pattern.

steps.title: Read a pressure–volume loop
steps.body: Ventricular filling, isovolumetric contraction, ejection and isovolumetric relaxation form an idealised cycle. The enclosed loop area represents external pressure–volume work per beat. Stroke volume is the difference between end-diastolic and end-systolic volumes, not the absolute volume at either corner.

steps.title: Connect electrical sequence
steps.body: The ECG records body-surface potential differences generated by cardiac electrical activity. P, QRS and T relate broadly to atrial depolarisation, ventricular depolarisation and ventricular repolarisation. Mechanical contraction follows electrical activation but is not directly drawn as voltage. Lead orientation affects waveform size and polarity.

steps.title: Work two checks
steps.body: For a simplified mean ejection pressure of 100 mmHg and stroke volume 70 mL, pressure times volume is roughly 0.93 J, an approximation to external work. For ideal limb-lead voltages with consistent sign convention, lead II = lead I + lead III. Check calibration before converting millimetres into time or millivolts.

question.prompt: What does the enclosed area of a ventricular pressure–volume loop represent?

options.reason: Cycle frequency is not the area of one pressure–volume loop.
Pressure integrated over volume change gives mechanical work.
The loop axes are pressure and volume, not voltage.

recall.prompt: Explain circulation, cardiac work and the ecg: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: Pressure integrated over volume change gives mechanical work. III = II − I = 1.0 − 0.3 = 0.7 mV. For a simplified mean ejection pressure of 100 mmHg and stroke volume 70 mL, pressure times volume is roughly 0.93 J, an approximation to external work. For ideal limb-lead voltages with consistent sign convention, lead II = lead I + lead III. Check calibration before converting millimetres into time or millivolts.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Breathing mechanics, gas exchange and physical examination
lessons.summary: Use pressure differences and volume definitions to explain quiet breathing.
lessons.section: Biophysics II, topic 36; combined theory prompts 304–314

steps.title: Separate the pressures
steps.body: Airflow depends on pressure difference between airway opening and alveoli. Transpulmonary pressure is alveolar minus pleural pressure and helps describe lung distension. It is not the pressure across the chest wall. Pleural pressure is normally subatmospheric during quiet breathing but need not always be negative.

steps.title: Follow a quiet breath
steps.body: Inspiratory muscle activity expands the thorax, changes pleural pressure and expands the lung; alveolar pressure falls slightly below atmospheric pressure during inward flow. Quiet expiration is mainly passive recoil. At moments of zero flow, alveolar pressure may equal atmospheric pressure even though the lung remains expanded.

steps.title: Define the volumes
steps.body: Tidal volume is the volume of an ordinary breath. Residual volume remains after maximal expiration. Functional residual capacity is the volume after an ordinary passive expiration: expiratory reserve volume plus residual volume. Spirometry alone cannot directly measure residual volume or capacities containing it.

steps.title: Connect mechanics and exchange
steps.body: Compliance is ΔV/ΔP over a specified range; resistance opposes flow. Restrictive and obstructive processes affect these differently. Henry's law links dissolved gas concentration to partial pressure through a gas–liquid-specific coefficient. Diffusion, ventilation and perfusion all contribute to exchange, so no single volume establishes adequate gas transfer.

steps.title: Interpret examination physics
steps.body: Inspection observes motion; palpation senses mechanical transmission; percussion probes the response of tissue and air-containing structures to an impulse; auscultation listens to sound generated and transmitted through the system. None gives a unique diagnosis from one sound. If ERV = 1.0 L and RV = 1.2 L, FRC = 2.2 L.

question.prompt: Which expression defines functional residual capacity?

options.reason: FRC is the volume remaining after an ordinary expiration, not one breath's size.
That combination is inspiratory capacity.
FRC includes expiratory reserve volume and residual volume.

recall.prompt: Explain breathing mechanics, gas exchange and physical examination: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: FRC includes expiratory reserve volume and residual volume. Relaxation of inspiratory muscles permits elastic recoil to drive outward flow. Inspection observes motion; palpation senses mechanical transmission; percussion probes the response of tissue and air-containing structures to an impulse; auscultation listens to sound generated and transmitted through the system. None gives a unique diagnosis from one sound. If ERV = 1.0 L and RV = 1.2 L, FRC = 2.2 L.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Practical: lens power and microscope calibration
lessons.summary: Solve image and calibration problems while keeping units and sign conventions visible.
lessons.section: Combined notes, practical questions 1–13

steps.title: Set up the measurement
steps.body: Record focal length in metres before using P = 1/f. For image distance, state the thin-lens sign convention and place object, lens and focal points on a sketch. The 17 mm focal length of a simplified optical system corresponds to about 58.8 D, not 0.0588 D.

steps.title: Calibrate the eyepiece
steps.body: An eyepiece scale has arbitrary divisions until compared with a stage micrometer. If 40 eyepiece divisions span 100 μm, each division represents 2.5 μm for that objective and configuration. Changing the objective requires a new calibration; changing magnification is not a licence to reuse the old conversion.

steps.title: Work an unknown length
steps.body: A structure spanning 12 calibrated divisions is 30 μm in this example. Repeat measurements across suitable boundaries and report meaningful precision. A thick or oblique section can change apparent size independently of the optical calibration.

steps.title: Predict before calculating
steps.body: For a converging lens, an object beyond twice the focal length produces a reduced real image. Between one and two focal lengths it produces an enlarged real image. Inside the focal length it produces a virtual enlarged image; exactly at the focus is the parallel-ray limiting case.

question.prompt: 40 eyepiece divisions equal 100 μm. How long is a 20-division object?

options.reason: Each division is 100/40 = 2.5 μm, not 10 μm.
Divide the calibration length by its division count before scaling.

recall.prompt: Explain lens power and microscope calibration: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: 20 × 2.5 μm = 50 μm. Calibration belongs to the optical configuration used for measurement. For a converging lens, an object beyond twice the focal length produces a reduced real image. Between one and two focal lengths it produces an enlarged real image. Inside the focal length it produces a virtual enlarged image; exactly at the focus is the parallel-ray limiting case.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Practical: refractive index and concentration
lessons.summary: Read a refractometer result as a calibrated, condition-dependent measurement.
lessons.section: Combined notes, practical questions 14–21

steps.title: Identify the principle
steps.body: An Abbe refractometer relates a boundary angle to sample refractive index using prisms of known optical properties. The light–dark boundary is a measurement feature, not a molecular image. Dispersion compensation helps compare wavelengths when using suitable illumination.

steps.title: Control the conditions
steps.body: Refractive index depends on wavelength, temperature and composition. A concentration estimate therefore requires a calibration for the relevant mixture under matching conditions. A water reference is not a universal constant equal to exactly one; that value is approximately for air relative to vacuum.

steps.title: Use a calibration
steps.body: Suppose a validated local calibration is n = 1.333 + 0.0015c with c in the calibration's stated concentration units. A reading of 1.348 gives c = (1.348 − 1.333)/0.0015 = 10 units. The numerical relation cannot be transferred to an unrelated solute without evidence.

steps.title: Judge the uncertainty
steps.body: A temperature drift or poorly defined boundary can shift the reading without a true concentration change. Record the calibration, temperature and wavelength specification with the result. For a nonlinear calibration curve, interpolate within the measured range rather than extrapolating a straight line indefinitely.

question.prompt: Using n = 1.333 + 0.0015c, a reading of 1.363 gives c…

options.reason: Subtract the intercept and divide by the calibration slope.
The index difference must be divided by the slope.

recall.prompt: Explain refractive index and concentration: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: Subtract the intercept and divide by the calibration slope. A valid concentration comparison requires matched or corrected measurement conditions. A temperature drift or poorly defined boundary can shift the reading without a true concentration change. Record the calibration, temperature and wavelength specification with the result. For a nonlinear calibration curve, interpolate within the measured range rather than extrapolating a straight line indefinitely.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Practical: blanks, dilution and absorbance
lessons.summary: Convert transmission into absorbance and design a defensible concentration measurement.
lessons.section: Combined notes, practical questions 22–32

steps.title: Establish the reference
steps.body: Measure a blank containing the appropriate solvent and container contribution. Then compare sample intensity I with blank intensity I₀. Use A = −log₁₀(I/I₀), taking transmission as a fraction rather than a percentage. A monochromator selects a wavelength range; it does not remove every instrumental error.

steps.title: Compare two samples
steps.body: Absorbance 1 means 10% transmission and absorbance 3 means 0.1%. The second transmits 100 times less light, although its absorbance is only three times as large. Under Beer–Lambert assumptions, concentration is proportional to absorbance at fixed wavelength and path length.

steps.title: Work a dilution
steps.body: A fivefold diluted sample has A = 0.40, and the calibration gives concentration 2 units per absorbance unit. Diluted concentration is 0.80 units; original concentration is 4.0 units. Apply the dilution factor after using the calibration, and keep concentration units consistent.

steps.title: Recognise failed assumptions
steps.body: Stray light, turbidity, chemical changes and detector limits can bend a calibration. A reading beyond the validated range should prompt suitable dilution or method review. A blank cannot make a scattering suspension behave like an ideal clear solution.

question.prompt: Absorbance changes from 1 to 3. Transmission changes by…

options.reason: Absorbance is logarithmic, so transmission does not follow its simple ratio.
Higher absorbance means lower transmission.
10⁻³/10⁻¹ = 10⁻², or one hundredth.

recall.prompt: Explain blanks, dilution and absorbance: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: 10⁻³/10⁻¹ = 10⁻², or one hundredth. 0.6 × 10 = 6 concentration units. Stray light, turbidity, chemical changes and detector limits can bend a calibration. A reading beyond the validated range should prompt suitable dilution or method review. A blank cannot make a scattering suspension behave like an ideal clear solution.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Practical: optical rotation and chirality
lessons.summary: Distinguish optical rotation from absorption and use a polarimetric calibration.
lessons.section: Combined notes, practical questions 33–42

steps.title: Prepare a polarised reference
steps.body: A polariser produces a defined polarisation state; an analyser compares the emerging orientation. Optical activity rotates the plane of linearly polarised light in suitable chiral media. Linear, circular and elliptical polarisation describe field evolution, not different photon charges.

steps.title: State Biot's relation
steps.body: For suitable conditions, rotation α = [α]lc, with specific rotation [α], path length l and concentration c in the convention used by the calibration. Temperature and wavelength must be specified. Opposite enantiomers can rotate equally in opposite directions; a racemic mixture may cancel net rotation.

steps.title: Work a path change
steps.body: A sample rotates light by +8° in a 1 dm cell. Under the same conditions, a 2 dm cell gives +16°. If concentration also halves, the rotation returns to +8°. Keep the sign because clockwise and counterclockwise rotations should not be reduced to unsigned brightness values.

steps.title: Interpret a null result
steps.body: Zero net rotation does not prove that no chiral molecules are present. Opposite contributions may cancel, concentration may be too low, or the measurement may be unsuitable. A polarimeter alone also does not determine a molecule's complete three-dimensional structure.

question.prompt: Path length doubles while concentration halves. Ideal optical rotation…

options.reason: In α = [α]lc, multiplying l by 2 and c by 1/2 cancels.
Both path length and concentration must be included.
The product lc remains unchanged rather than vanishing.

recall.prompt: Explain optical rotation and chirality: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: In α = [α]lc, multiplying l by 2 and c by 1/2 cancels. A null net signal can reflect cancellation rather than absence of chiral species. Zero net rotation does not prove that no chiral molecules are present. Opposite contributions may cancel, concentration may be too low, or the measurement may be unsuitable. A polarimeter alone also does not determine a molecule's complete three-dimensional structure.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Practical: eye optics and visual acuity
lessons.summary: Relate refractive error and angular resolution to the eye's optical system.
lessons.section: Combined notes, practical questions 43–58

steps.title: Use a simplified eye
steps.body: The eye's combined optical power is often approximated near 60 D, with a major contribution from the cornea. Accommodation changes lens shape and power. This reduced-eye model is useful for reasoning but does not capture every refracting surface or individual variation.

steps.title: Locate the focus
steps.body: In myopia, parallel rays focus in front of the retina in the uncorrected relaxed eye; a diverging correction reduces effective convergence. In hyperopia, the relaxed focus would lie behind the retina; a converging correction can help. Presbyopia concerns reduced accommodation rather than being identical to either axial refractive error.

steps.title: Interpret acuity
steps.body: Acuity tests assess the smallest resolvable angular detail under defined conditions. If minimum resolvable angle is 2 arcminutes, decimal acuity under the conventional reciprocal relation is 0.5. Viewing distance, contrast and correct use of the chart matter; an acuity value alone does not measure all aspects of vision.

steps.title: Explain the blind spot
steps.body: The optic disc lacks photoreceptors where the nerve exits. A target can disappear at the corresponding visual-field position despite intact surrounding vision. This is anatomically different from optical blur caused by defocus, and it is not the same structure as the fovea.

question.prompt: What optical correction is used conceptually for myopia?

options.text: A lens that moves the retina physically
options.reason: A spectacle lens alters ray convergence, not retinal position.
Reducing convergence helps move the focus back toward the retina.

options.text: A converging lens that adds more positive power
options.reason: More convergence would move the relaxed focus farther in front of the retina.

recall.prompt: Explain eye optics and visual acuity: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: Reducing convergence helps move the focus back toward the retina. Decimal acuity is 1/2 = 0.5 for this convention. The optic disc lacks photoreceptors where the nerve exits. A target can disappear at the corresponding visual-field position despite intact surrounding vision. This is anatomically different from optical blur caused by defocus, and it is not the same structure as the fovea.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Practical: scintillation spectra and background
lessons.summary: Distinguish pulse height, energy calibration and count rate.
lessons.section: Combined notes, practical questions 59–66, 127–132

steps.title: Trace the chain
steps.body: Scintillator light produces photoelectrons, dynodes amplify them and electronics shape a pulse. A spectrum bins pulses by height; calibration relates channel to deposited energy. Increasing photomultiplier gain can shift a peak along the channel axis without changing the radionuclide's emission energy.

steps.title: Account for background
steps.body: Subtract expected background counts with an appropriate time scaling. For independent counts, variances add when subtracting. A discriminator can reject low pulses, but raising the threshold may remove true low-energy events as well as noise. Signal-to-noise improvement must be assessed, not assumed.

steps.title: Work a rate
steps.body: A sample-plus-background count of 1200 over 60 s gives 20 counts/s. Background 300 over 60 s gives 5 counts/s, so net rate is 15 counts/s. The uncertainty of the difference is based on both counts, approximately √1500/60 ≈ 0.65 counts/s in the simple Poisson model.

steps.title: Separate efficiency from activity
steps.body: A source with 1000 decays/s may produce far fewer detected counts because of geometry, branching and detector efficiency. Changing source distance alters count rate without changing physical activity. Dead time and pile-up complicate high-rate measurements and can distort both counts and spectral shapes.

question.prompt: Detector gain increases and a peak moves to a higher channel. The emitted photon energy…

options.text: Must have increased in the source
options.reason: Electronic amplification does not change nuclear transition energies.
A channel shift does not imply missing energy.
Gain changes the channel–energy mapping and requires suitable calibration.

recall.prompt: Explain scintillation spectra and background: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: Gain changes the channel–energy mapping and requires suitable calibration. Net rate is 30 − 8 = 22 counts/s. A source with 1000 decays/s may produce far fewer detected counts because of geometry, branching and detector efficiency. Changing source distance alters count rate without changing physical activity. Dead time and pile-up complicate high-rate measurements and can distort both counts and spectral shapes.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Practical: half-value layers and shielding curves
lessons.summary: Translate exponential attenuation into thickness while recognising beam assumptions.
lessons.section: Combined notes, practical questions 67–75

steps.title: Define attenuation quantities
steps.body: For a narrow monoenergetic beam in a uniform material, I/I₀ = exp(−μx). Linear attenuation coefficient μ has inverse-length units. Mass attenuation coefficient μ/ρ separates density, and areal density ρx has mass-per-area units. Absorption and removal from the direct beam are not identical.

steps.title: Use layer definitions
steps.body: Half-value layer is ln 2/μ; tenth-value layer is ln 10/μ. Two half-value layers leave one quarter and three leave one eighth. For a broad polyenergetic beam, scatter and beam hardening can prevent a single constant half-value layer from describing every depth.

steps.title: Work thickness
steps.body: If the half-value layer is 2 cm in the stated model, reducing direct intensity to 1/16 requires four layers, or 8 cm. This is a mathematical teaching example, not a shielding design specification. Actual shielding depends on the spectrum, geometry and regulatory context.

steps.title: Compare materials fairly
steps.body: Lead attenuation varies with photon energy; it has no universal percentage reduction per millimetre. Water and steam at the same thickness have different areal densities. At equal composition and appropriate energy, using mass thickness clarifies why density changes the linear attenuation.

question.prompt: Three half-value layers leave what direct-beam fraction?

options.reason: Each half-value layer halves the remaining direct beam, so three layers give (1/2)³ = 1/8.
Each layer halves the remaining beam.
Attenuation cannot increase the direct beam under this model.

recall.prompt: Explain half-value layers and shielding curves: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: (1/2)³ = 1/8. cm⁻¹ multiplied by cm gives a dimensionless exponent. Lead attenuation varies with photon energy; it has no universal percentage reduction per millimetre. Water and steam at the same thickness have different areal densities. At equal composition and appropriate energy, using mass thickness clarifies why density changes the linear attenuation.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Practical: oscillations, damping and resonance
lessons.summary: Predict frequency changes and interpret a driven oscillator's response.
lessons.section: Combined notes, practical questions 76–83

steps.title: Start with an ideal oscillator
steps.body: For a mass on an ideal spring, f = (1/2π)√(k/m). Displacement, velocity and acceleration have related but different phases. The model requires small motion in a linear spring regime; a biological structure may be nonlinear or have several modes.

steps.title: Add damping and driving
steps.body: Damping dissipates mechanical energy and reduces free-oscillation amplitude. Periodic forcing produces a frequency-dependent response, with resonance shaped by damping. Greater damping usually broadens and lowers the resonance peak. Resonance does not mean a device produces energy without external input.

steps.title: Work a change
steps.body: Doubling mass at fixed k multiplies frequency by 1/√2 ≈ 0.707. Doubling k at fixed mass multiplies frequency by √2. A cantilever can act as a mechanical sensor because changes in effective stiffness or mass affect its oscillation response.

steps.title: Read a decay curve
steps.body: An exponentially decaying amplitude should not be confused with the energy envelope: in a simple harmonic mode, energy scales with amplitude squared. A halved amplitude therefore corresponds to one quarter of the oscillation energy under the same stiffness.

question.prompt: Mass quadruples at unchanged spring stiffness. Frequency…

options.reason: The square root makes the factor one half.
f scales as 1/√m, so a fourfold mass halves frequency.
Mass appears in the denominator inside the square root.

recall.prompt: Explain oscillations, damping and resonance: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: f scales as 1/√m, so a fourfold mass halves frequency. The energy ratio is (1/2)² = 1/4. An exponentially decaying amplitude should not be confused with the energy envelope: in a simple harmonic mode, energy scales with amplitude squared. A halved amplitude therefore corresponds to one quarter of the oscillation energy under the same stiffness.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Practical: resistance, capacitance and biological impedance
lessons.summary: Explain why tissue response depends on signal frequency and electrode arrangement.
lessons.section: Combined notes, practical questions 84–93

steps.title: Separate electrical quantities
steps.body: Resistance relates voltage and current for an ideal resistor, V = IR. Resistivity also accounts for geometry through R = ρL/A. A capacitor stores separated charge, Q = CV, and has capacitive reactance magnitude Xc = 1/(2πfC). Reactance introduces a phase relationship as well as a magnitude.

steps.title: Model a membrane or skin interface
steps.body: An RC equivalent circuit can represent some frequency-dependent behaviour, but real tissue and electrode interfaces are more complex. Higher frequency reduces capacitive reactance. Electrode placement, contact quality and geometry influence a measured impedance; it is not an intrinsic tissue number independent of the method.

steps.title: Work a frequency change
steps.body: For C = 1 μF at f = 1000 Hz, Xc ≈ 159 Ω. At 2000 Hz it is about 79.6 Ω. An ideal capacitor blocks steady DC after charging but can carry changing current; this does not mean charge crosses its insulating layer as in a resistor.

steps.title: Distinguish peak and RMS
steps.body: For a sinusoidal voltage, Vrms = Vpeak/√2. Resistive power uses Vrms²/R for that waveform. Combining peak voltage with an RMS power formula produces a factor-of-two error. Classroom circuit equations do not establish safe currents or electrode procedures for use on people.

question.prompt: Frequency doubles for an ideal capacitor. Reactance magnitude…

options.reason: Frequency is in the denominator of 1/(2πfC).
Capacitive reactance is frequency dependent.
Doubling f halves Xc at fixed capacitance.

recall.prompt: Explain resistance, capacitance and biological impedance: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: Doubling f halves Xc at fixed capacitance. 10/√2 ≈ 7.07 V. For a sinusoidal voltage, Vrms = Vpeak/√2. Resistive power uses Vrms²/R for that waveform. Combining peak voltage with an RMS power formula produces a factor-of-two error. Classroom circuit equations do not establish safe currents or electrode procedures for use on people.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Practical: gain, decibels and bandwidth
lessons.summary: Use gain ratios correctly and recognise when amplification loses information.
lessons.section: Combined notes, practical questions 94–103

steps.title: Define the ratio
steps.body: Voltage gain is output voltage divided by input voltage. For a voltage ratio, gain in decibels is 20 log₁₀|Vout/Vin|; interpreting that as power gain requires appropriate impedance conditions. Power ratios use 10 log₁₀(Pout/Pin). A decibel value needs its reference and quantity.

steps.title: Read a frequency response
steps.body: Amplifier gain can vary with frequency. Bandwidth identifies a useful range under a stated criterion, commonly relative to a midband level. Negative feedback can improve stability and linearity while changing gain and bandwidth. It cannot recover information already clipped at an earlier stage.

steps.title: Work a gain
steps.body: A 2 mV input becomes 200 mV, giving voltage gain 100 and 40 dB. A further stage with gain 10 gives total gain 1000, or 60 dB. Linear gains multiply, while their decibel values add when defined consistently.

steps.title: Check clipping and loading
steps.body: A signal that exceeds available output range clips, distorting the waveform and adding spectral components. A voltage divider's output also changes when a load draws current. Write down input range, output limit and loading assumptions before treating an amplifier as a perfect multiplier.

question.prompt: A voltage gain of 10 corresponds to…

options.reason: 20 log₁₀10 = 20 dB.
Voltage gain uses 20 log₁₀ of the ratio.
Decibel gain is logarithmic, not the square of the ratio.

recall.prompt: Explain gain, decibels and bandwidth: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: 20 log₁₀10 = 20 dB. The first multiplies by 5 and the second by 4, giving 20. A signal that exceeds available output range clips, distorting the waveform and adding spectral components. A voltage divider's output also changes when a load draws current. Write down input range, output limit and loading assumptions before treating an amplifier as a perfect multiplier.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Practical: electrical cell counting
lessons.summary: Connect an impedance pulse to particle volume and identify coincidence errors.
lessons.section: Combined notes, practical questions 104–111

steps.title: Explain the aperture
steps.body: In a Coulter-type measurement, particles suspended in conducting electrolyte pass through a small aperture. A particle displaces conducting liquid and changes electrical resistance, producing a pulse. Under calibrated conditions, pulse size relates to displaced volume, while pulse count relates to the number of detected passages.

steps.title: Control the suspension
steps.body: An appropriate electrolyte and suspension preserve meaningful particle behaviour. Dilution reduces the chance that two particles occupy the sensing region together. Debris, aggregation and particles outside the calibrated range can distort a distribution; the instrument does not identify every cell type from volume alone.

steps.title: Work a dilution correction
steps.body: A diluted sample yields 200 counted particles per μL after the instrument's volume calculation. With a 100-fold dilution, the original estimate is 20,000 per μL. This assumes representative mixing, correct sampled volume and negligible unresolved coincidence.

steps.title: Interpret coincidence
steps.body: Two cells passing together may generate one larger event, biasing both count and apparent size. Lowering concentration can test whether coincidence contributes. A histogram peak is a population pattern, not proof that every event represents one normal cell.

question.prompt: What most directly influences pulse height in a calibrated Coulter measurement?

options.reason: The method senses an electrical displacement effect, not sequence.
Pulse amplitude is related to the volume displacing conducting electrolyte.

options.text: Only the number of cells in the entire tube
options.reason: Total sample count and individual pulse height are different measurements.

recall.prompt: Explain electrical cell counting: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.
recall.answer: Pulse amplitude is related to the volume displacing conducting electrolyte. Reduced concentration lowers coincidence probability under suitable counting conditions. Two cells passing together may generate one larger event, biasing both count and apparent size. Lowering concentration can test whether coincidence contributes. A histogram peak is a population pattern, not proof that every event represents one normal cell.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Practical: diffusion slopes and uncertainty
lessons.summary: Calculate a diffusion scale and explain why a straight-line plot needs a model.
lessons.section: Combined notes, practical questions 112–116

steps.title: Choose the observed quantity
steps.body: For one-dimensional free diffusion, ⟨x²⟩ = 2Dt, so a mean-squared-displacement versus time slope estimates 2D. A concentration profile requires a different fit and suitable boundary conditions. Individual trajectories fluctuate; one displacement is not the ensemble average.

steps.title: Work a scale
steps.body: With D = 2 × 10⁻¹⁰ m²/s and t = 1 s, root-mean-square displacement is √(2Dt) = 2 × 10⁻⁵ m, or 20 μm. At 4 s it is 40 μm. The distance grows with the square root of time, not linearly.

steps.title: Test the interpretation
steps.body: Drift adds directed motion and can make a simple diffusion estimate misleading. Temperature, viscosity, particle size, confinement and binding also matter. In an optical concentration experiment, converting signal into concentration introduces calibration uncertainty before the transport model is fitted.

steps.title: Compare transport routes
steps.body: Convection carries material with bulk flow; diffusion reflects random motion and concentration redistribution. A membrane may add a permeability barrier rather than merely extending a free-fluid distance. State which region and transport mechanism the measured coefficient describes.

question.prompt: For 1D diffusion, the slope of mean squared displacement versus time is…

options.reason: The standard relation is ⟨x²⟩ = 2Dt.
Faster diffusion produces a larger, not inverse, slope.
Differentiating ⟨x²⟩ = 2Dt gives slope 2D.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Practical: sound levels and audiograms
lessons.summary: Distinguish physical sound level from a frequency-dependent hearing threshold.
lessons.section: Combined notes, practical questions 133–142

steps.title: Use a reference
steps.body: Intensity level is 10 log₁₀(I/Iref). Sound-pressure level uses 20 log₁₀(prms/pref) under the corresponding acoustic conditions. A 10 dB intensity-level increase means ten times the intensity, not necessarily ten times perceived loudness. A level without its reference is incomplete.

steps.title: Read the axes
steps.body: An audiogram plots hearing threshold against frequency using a specified hearing-level reference. It does not directly plot a sound wave or the cochlear displacement. Test conditions and masking can matter when distinguishing responses of the two ears; a curve alone should not be treated as a full diagnosis.

steps.title: Compare perception
steps.body: Equal-loudness contours show frequency dependence of perception. Phon compares loudness with a 1 kHz tone; sone expresses relative loudness. In the conventional relation above the reference region, a 10-phon increase corresponds approximately to doubled sones, distinct from the physical intensity ratio.

steps.title: Work a level difference
steps.body: An intensity rises from I to 100I, giving a 20 dB increase. If RMS pressure doubles in the same medium, sound-pressure level rises by about 6 dB. These two examples use different underlying ratios, which is why their logarithmic multipliers differ.

question.prompt: Intensity increases by a factor of 100. Level rises by…

options.reason: 10 log₁₀100 = 20 dB.
Intensity level uses the logarithm of the ratio.
The 20 multiplier applies to a pressure ratio, not this intensity ratio.

recall.prompt: Explain sound levels and audiograms: state the mechanism, work an example and name one assumption.

If RMS pressure doubles in the same medium, sound-pressure level rises by about 6 dB. These two examples use different underlying ratios, which is why their logarithmic multipliers differ.

lessons.subject: biophysics
lessons.title: Practical: ECG calibration and pulse timing
lessons.summary: Convert a recorded trace into voltage and time, and distinguish pulse-generator behaviours.
lessons.section: Combined notes, practical questions 143–157

steps.title: Read calibration first
steps.body: An ECG trace needs both voltage and paper-speed calibration. At 10 mm/mV, a 12 mm deflection represents 1.2 mV. At 25 mm/s, a 2 mm interval is 0.08 s. These are measurement exercises; voltage or timing alone is insufficient for a clinical interpretation.

steps.title: Compare leads and rejection
steps.body: Standard limb leads obey II = I + III in the ideal consistent-sign description. Differential amplifiers measure a voltage difference and aim to reject common-mode interference. Poor contact and motion can still introduce artifacts; a large recorded deflection need not reflect a larger cardiac source.

steps.title: Classify pulse behaviour
steps.body: An astable circuit oscillates without a stable resting state, a monostable returns to its stable state after a triggered pulse, and a bistable has two stable states. These concepts help explain timing electronics. A conceptual pulse exercise is not an instruction to construct or program a pacemaker.

steps.title: Work a pulse train
steps.body: A period of 1 s gives frequency 1 Hz. A pulse lasting 2 ms every second has duty cycle 0.2%. For an ideal rectangular voltage pulse across a resistor, energy is V²t/R. Shape, load and safety controls matter in real devices, so this ideal expression is used only for the classroom model.

question.prompt: At 25 mm/s, a 5 mm interval corresponds to…

options.reason: Millimetres are not seconds without applying the calibration.
5 mm divided by 25 mm/s equals 0.20 s.
Divide length by speed: 5/25 seconds.

A pulse lasting 2 ms every second has duty cycle 0.2%. For an ideal rectangular voltage pulse across a resistor, energy is V²t/R. Shape, load and safety controls matter in real devices, so this ideal expression is used only for the classroom model.
